body:
[Lem 76 (Kolmogorov continuity lemma for distributions) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $(t,\phi) \mapsto V(t,\phi)$ be a map from $[0,T]\times \mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ into $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ which is linear and continuous in $\phi$. Fix a non-negative integer $r$. Assume there exists some $\kappa>0, q>d/\kappa$ and $\alpha<-r$ and $C=C(\kappa,\alpha,q,{T})>0$ such that 
		\begin{align*}\mE[|V(t,S^\lambda_{x}\phi)|^q]^{1/q}&\leq C\lambda^{\alpha },\\  \mE[|V(t,S^\lambda_{x}\phi)-V(s,S^\lambda_{x}\phi)|^q]^{1/q}&\leq C\lambda^{\alpha -\kappa} |t-s|^{\kappa },
		\end{align*}uniformly over all smooth functions $\phi$ on $\mathbb R$ supported on the unit ball of $\mathbb R$ with {$\|\phi\|_{C^r}\leq 1$}, and uniformly over $\lambda\in(0,1]$ and $0\leq s,t\leq T$. Then for any $\tau>1$ and any $\beta<\alpha-\kappa$ there exists a random variable $\big(\mathscr V(t)\big)_{t\in[0,T]}$ taking values in $C([0,T],C^{\beta,\tau}(\mathbb R^d))$ such that $(\mathscr V(t),\phi)=V(t,\phi)$ almost surely for all $\phi$ and $t$. Furthermore, one has that $$\mE[\|\mathscr V\|^q_{C([0,T],C^{\beta,\tau}(\mathbb R^d))}]\leq C',$$ where $C'$ depends on the choice of $\alpha,\beta,q,\kappa,$ and the constant $C$ appearing in the moment bound above but not on $V,\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Kolmogorov continuity lemma for distributions

[Lemma lem:feature-conjugacy of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $\widetilde b_j$ be the columns of $\widetilde B$, and let $b_j^H$ be the columns of $B_H$.  Define
\[
        \widetilde f_j(y)
        :=\operatorname{div}_y\widetilde b_j(y)-\widetilde b_j(y)\cdot\nabla\widetilde V(y),
\]
and
\[
        f_j^H(x)
        :=\operatorname{div}_x b_j^H(x)-b_j^H(x)\cdot\nabla V_H(x).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
        f_j^H(H(y))=\widetilde f_j(y),
        \qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $\rho_H=H_{\#}\widetilde\rho$, then
\begin{equation}
        \rho_H F_H=\widetilde\rho\,\widetilde F.
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:rho-convexity-subcritical-interval-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume the vector law is energy-admissible. Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For \(0<q\le1\), one has 
\(
\rho(q)<\infty
\).

\item The function 
\(
q\mapsto \log_2\rho(q)
\)
is convex on every interval on which 
\(
\rho(q)<\infty
\).

\item One has
\[
\rho(1)=1,
\qquad
\left.\frac{d}{dq}\right|_{q=1-}\log_2\rho(q)=\gamma(X)<0.
\]

\item For every \(0<q<1\), one has \(\rho(q)>1.\)

\item The set
\[
I_X=\{q\in(1,2):\rho(q)<1\}
\]
is either empty or an initial interval of \((1,2)\), namely one of
\[
(1,q_*),\qquad (1,q_*],\qquad (1,2),
\]
where \(q_*\in(1,2)\) in the first two cases.

[Definition 16 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] A $\cV$-valued optional process
$u=(u_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$
is called a solution of \eqref{SNS5}--\eqref{div5}--\eqref{bin5} on $[0,T]$ if
$u\in L_2([0,T],\cV)\cap L_\infty([0,T],\cH)$ (a.s.),  
and for every $\varphi\in\cV$, 
\begin{align}
(u_t,\varphi)=&(u_0,\varphi)-
\int_0^t\Big[\big(a_s^{ij}D_j u_s+\frf_s^i(u_s),D_i \varphi\big)
+(u_{s(u_s)},\varphi)\Big]\,ds                                                                   \nonumber\\
&+\int_0^t\big(\gamma_s^{ki}D_i q_s^k+f_s(u_s,Du_s),\varphi\big)\,ds  \nonumber\\
&+\int_0^t\big(\sigma_s^{ik}D_i u_s+h_s^k(u_s),\varphi\big)\,dw_s^k    \nonumber\\
&+\int_0^{t}\int_{Z}\big(\frh_s(u_{s-},z),\varphi\big)\,\tilde\pi(ds,dz)                       
\end{align}
holds for $\mathbb P\otimes dt$-almost every
$(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T]$. In addition 
equation \eqref{pressure_assumption} is assumed to hold. 

As before, we call
$u=(u_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$
an $\cH$-solution if it is an $\cH$-valued 
$\cF_t$-adapted c\`adl\`ag process such that
$u\in L_2([0,T],\cV)\ \text{(a.s.)}$, 
almost surely \eqref{1.19.6} holds for all
$t\in[0,T],\,\varphi\in\mathcal V$, 
and equation \eqref{pressure_assumption} is satisfied. 
Recall that a solution is called an admissible solution if it is 
an admissible function.
title: Definition 16 of arXiv:2606.29512

Fix a positive integer k and a constant mu in(0,1). For integer d>=k, let U_d be uniform on{-1,1}^d and let P_mu have independent binary coordinates of mean mu. For0<=rho<=1 set D=(1-rho)*U_d+rho*P_mu. Let P_F be uniform over the binom(d,k) parity functions chi_S(x)=product_{j in S}x_j with |S|=k. There exists C_k>0 depending only on k such that, for all sufficiently large d (the threshold may depend on k and mu), uniformly over rho in[0,1], CP_infinity(P_F,D)<=1/binom(d,k)+C_k*rho^2*mu^(4k). Here CP_infinity is the average squared D-correlation of two independent P_F draws. This is a fixed-k asymptotic interpretation of source Lemma16; no degree-uniform constant for k=k(d) is supplied.
Fixed k>=1 and fixed0<mu<1; d tends to infinity.
Two supports are sampled independently and uniformly among all k-subsets.
Input mixture weight0<=rho<=1; product coordinates have common mean mu.

Let $(Z_1,Z_2)$ be standard bivariate normal with correlation $\rho \in [-1,1]$, and write $z_+=\max\{z,0\}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[(Z_1)_+(Z_2)_+] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\left(\sqrt{1-\rho^2}+(\pi-\arccos\rho)\,\rho\right)$. At $\rho=1$ this gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_+^2]=\tfrac12=\tfrac12\mathbb{E}[Z^2]$, and at $\rho=0$ it gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_+]^2=1/(2\pi)$. The normalized map $\rho \mapsto 2\pi\,\mathbb{E}[(Z_1)_+(Z_2)_+]/\pi$ has derivative $1$ at $\rho=1^-$, so the correlation dynamics it induces is marginal at perfect correlation. This is the degree-one arc-cosine kernel; sources defining that kernel often carry a compensating factor of two, so the constant should be checked against the convention in use rather than copied.
(Z_1,Z_2) is centered bivariate normal with unit variances and correlation rho

The integrand is nonnegative exactly on the arc of angular width $\\pi-\\theta$ where both cosines are positive, and integrating $\\cos\\phi\\cos(\\phi-\\theta)$ over that arc gives $\\tfrac12((\\pi-\\theta)\\cos\\theta+\\sin\\theta)$. [Prop prop_parity of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S$ be an APS and let $\triangle v$ be a one-variable APS term. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $d(\triangle)$ is even, then $\triangle v$ is an order-preserving operation on $L$. 
    That is, for any $x, y \in L$, $x \leq y$ implies $\triangle x \leq \triangle y$. 

    \item If $d(\triangle)$ is odd, then $\triangle v$ is an order-reversing operation on $L$. 
    That is, for any $x, y \in L$, $x \leq y$ implies $\triangle y \leq \triangle x$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A partially ordered set (poset) is a pair (P, <=) where <= is a binary relation on P that is reflexive (x <= x), antisymmetric (x <= y and y <= x implies x = y), and transitive (x <= y and y <= z implies x <= z). A subset C of P is a chain if every two elements of C are comparable, that is, for all x, y in C, x <= y or y <= x. A subset A of P is an antichain if no two distinct elements of A are comparable. [standard, e.g. Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1]
title: Partially Ordered Set, Chain, and Antichain

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed. Let X in R^(p-by-r) satisfy X^T X=I_r with p>r>=1, and let M be SPD r-by-r. On T_X St(p,r), set g_R(xi,xi)=tr(xi^T xi M). For any SPD p-by-p A, set g_A(xi,xi)=tr(xi^T A xi), and let c_A,C_A be the infimum and supremum of g_A/g_R over nonzero tangent vectors. Then C_A/c_A >= kappa(M), and equality is attained for every A=a I_p, a>0. Thus the optimal ambient-row metric distortion is exactly kappa(M); proportional representation on the entire tangent space is possible iff M is scalar. For p=r>=2 this obstruction disappears: A=X M X^T represents g_R exactly. This concerns metric comparison, not algorithmic iteration lower bounds or Gaussian LoRA convergence.

M SPD r-by-r; A SPD p-by-p, allowed to depend on X

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a7083406f33c5a057a0bc3f88c5afe6fa80bf5d0c1c4eae070a3db5f9de683e0","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a7/a7083406f33c5a057a0bc3f88c5afe6fa80bf5d0c1c4eae070a3db5f9de683e0.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:162562ad4878057f1e3c2d3f8f129b53522d4f66a642b4132d98a03923fdaec7","bundle_entry_key":"stiefel-metric-distortion","bundle_id":"population.t419-stiefel-optimal-metric-distortion-021","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Stiefel manifold metric comparison","draft":"w705/bundle_021.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.riemannian:stiefel-column-weight-ambient-row-optimal-metric-distortion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C035 v1: exact distortion of column-to-row metric transfer

Kind: route-failure. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited).
This is an auxiliary geometric obstruction, not a LoRA iteration lower bound,
new convergence regime, or claim of novelty. The hardest remaining piece is
a quantitative Gaussian entry time for the actual C029 dynamics.

Let X be a real p-by-r matrix with X^T X=I_r, where p>r>=1.
Let M be SPD r-by-r. At X the Stiefel tangent space is
T={xi: X^T xi+xi^T X=0}. Define

    g_R(xi,xi)=tr(xi^T xi M),
    g_A(xi,xi)=tr(xi^T A xi),

where A is any SPD p-by-p matrix. It may depend on X; the assertion is
pointwise. Let c_A and C_A be respectively the infimum and supremum of
g_A(xi,xi)/g_R(xi,xi) over nonzero xi in T. Both are positive and finite
by compactness of a unit sphere in this nonzero finite-dimensional space.
Write kappa(M)=lambda_max(M)/lambda_min(M).

**Theorem.** C_A/c_A >= kappa(M) for every A. Equality is attained by
every A=a I_p, a>0. Consequently the optimal distortion over ambient-row
SPD metrics is exactly kappa(M). A metric proportional to g_R can be
represented by an ambient-row SPD metric on the entire tangent space
if and only if M is scalar.

**Proof.** Since p>r there is a unit v with X^T v=0. For every nonzero
z in R^r, xi=v z^T is tangent, and direct multiplication gives

    g_A(xi,xi)/g_R(xi,xi)=(v^T A v) ||z||^2/(z^T M z).

Taking z to be unit eigenvectors for lambda_max(M) and lambda_min(M)
shows c_A <= (v^T A v)/lambda_max(M) and
C_A >= (v^T A v)/lambda_min(M). Their quotient is at least kappa(M).
For A=a I_p, the eigenvalue bounds on M imply that all tangent ratios
are between a/lambda_max(M) and a/lambda_min(M). The same two rank-one
directions attain the endpoints. This proves optimality. Proportionality
would give distortion one, forcing kappa(M)=1. Conversely if M=m I_r,
take A=m I_p to obtain equality of the two metrics. QED.

**Why the strict dimension hypothesis matters.** For p=r and r>=2,
X is orthogonal and tangent vectors have the form xi=X Omega with
Omega skew-symmetric. In this case A=X M X^T represents g_R exactly:

    g_A=tr(Omega^T M Omega)=tr(M Omega Omega^T),
    g_R=tr(Omega^T Omega M).

Since Omega Omega^T=Omega^T Omega, these quadratic forms agree, and
polarization gives agreement of their bilinear forms. Thus the proper
bottleneck hypothesis cannot be discarded. For p=r=1 the tangent space
is zero and a nonzero-vector distortion quotient is not defined.

**Application and limit.** C029's row-frame metric tr(dY^T M dY), after
X=Y^T, is g_R. Shustin--Avron's equation (3.10) (arXiv1902.01635v4,
PDF p9, as checked in C034) is of ambient-row form. For a proper
bottleneck, identifying these metrics without a condition-number loss
is impossible unless M is scalar. This statement concerns comparison
constants for metrics only. It does not imply a lower bound on the
iterations of any particular algorithm or exclude other transfers of
the primary source's techniques. Neither target is solved.

Sources: direct tangent-space and trace calculation above; C034 for the
primary source's metric convention. Independent audit and novelty

Let 0 < alpha < 1 and let Omega in R^n be a bounded C^{2,alpha} domain. Let Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u be strictly elliptic in Omega (sum a^{ij} xi_i xi_j >= lambda|xi|^2, lambda > 0) with a^{ij} = a^{ji} and all coefficients in C^{0,alpha}(closure of Omega) with norms at most Lambda. (a) A priori estimate: if u in C^{2,alpha}(closure of Omega) satisfies Lu = f in Omega and u = g on the boundary with f in C^{0,alpha}(closure of Omega) and g in C^{2,alpha}(closure of Omega), then ||u||_{C^{2,alpha}(closure of Omega)} <= C ( sup |u| + ||g||_{C^{2,alpha}} + ||f||_{C^{0,alpha}} ) with C = C(n, alpha, lambda, Lambda, Omega). (b) If moreover c <= 0 in Omega, then the Dirichlet problem Lu = f in Omega, u = g on the boundary, has exactly one solution u in C^{2,alpha}(closure of Omega), and the term sup|u| in (a) may be dropped, because the maximum principle gives sup |u| <= sup over the boundary of |g| + C(diam Omega, lambda, sup|b|) sup |f|.

body:
[Prop 5 of arXiv:2604.02129, 'Realisation of constraints in underdamped Langevin dynamics'] Given $\eps>0$, let $(Q_t,P_t)$ be the solution to~\eqref{eq:abc-slow},\eqref{eq:intro-0Mass-Fast}, with corresponding initial data $(Q^i_0,P^i_0)$ for $i=1,2$. Recall the definition of the potential $V$ from~\eqref{eq:Valpha} and the parameter $\alpha\geq 0$. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item 
        For any $t\geq 0$ 
        \begin{align}
          
            \E\Bigl[|P_t^{1}|^2\Bigr] \leq 
            \begin{dcases} C_1 \bigl(\eps +  e^{-\frac{C_2}{\eps}t} |P_0^{1}|^2\bigr) \  &\text{if $\alpha=0$}, \\
            C_3 \left(\eps +\eps |Q^1_0|^2  + (e^{-\frac{C_4}{\eps}t} + \eps)  |P^1_0|^2    \right) &\text{if $\alpha>0$},
             \end{dcases}
        \end{align}
        where the constants $C_1, C_2, C_3, C_4>0$ are independent of $\eps$ and $t$.

        \item Let $(\hat q_t,q_t,p_t)\in \R^{k}\times \R^{d-k} \times \R^{d-k}$ with initial data $(\hat q_0,q_0,p_0)=(Q^1_0,Q^2_0,P^2_0)$  evolve according to~\eqref{eq:0Mass-q1} and~\eqref{eq:limit-gen}. 
        We have for any $t\leq 0$
        \begin{align}
        \E\biggl[\Bigl|(Q^{1}_t,Q^{2}_t,P^{2}_t)^\top - (\hat q_t,q_t,p_t)^\top\Bigr|^2\biggr] \leq \begin{dcases}C_5 e^{C_6 t^2}\Bigl(\eps + 
        \bigl|P_0^{1}\bigr|^2  \Bigr) \ &\text{if $\alpha=0$}, \\
        C_7 e^{C_8 t^2}\Bigl(\eps t^2+\eps^2 t^2 \bigl|Q_0^{1}\bigr|^2 + |P^1_0|^2\Bigr)  &\text{if $\alpha>0$},
        \end{dcases}
        \end{align}
        where the constants $C_5,C_6, C_7,C_8>0$ are independent of $\eps>0$ and $t>0$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Invariant monotone coupling under an amenable action Result: Start with a monotone coupling of the two invariant forest laws under a countable amenable action. Average its translates over a Folner sequence. The product space of two edge configurations is compact, the prescribed marginals are unchanged, and the order relation is closed. A subsequential weak limit is therefore still a monotone coupling and is invariant because translation changes each average by at most its Folner boundary ratio. Check: The argument averages probability measures, not individual configurations, so convexity preserves the marginals and the monotone support. Compactness is available for a countable locally finite edge set. Obstruction: For a nonamenable acting group there is no Folner averaging sequence. Existence of an arbitrary monotone coupling does not by itself produce an invariant one.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0044-invariant-monotone-coupling-of-free-and-wired-uniform-spanning-forests
No independent review

Let n>=2, alpha in (0,1], and A be an n x n symmetric random matrix with A_ii=0 and mutually independent upper-triangular entries A_ij~Bernoulli(p_ij). Set P=E A. Suppose p_ij<=alpha and there exist 0<nbar_min<=nbar_max such that alpha nbar_min<=sum_j p_ij<=alpha nbar_max for every i. Write mu=nbar_max/nbar_min. For a nonnegative symmetric matrix B define L(B)=D(B)^(-1/2) B D(B)^(-1/2), where D(B)_ii=sum_j B_ij and inverse square roots at zero degrees are zero. For every nu>0 there exist constants C_nu,Cprime_nu depending only on nu such that, if alpha>=Cprime_nu mu log(n)/nbar_min, then P(||L(A)-L(P)||_op <= C_nu mu sqrt(n)/(nbar_min sqrt(alpha)))>=1-n^(-nu). This normalized matrix is adjacency normalization, not I minus the normalized adjacency. The constants do not give convergence for a general bounded-degree static graph sequence.
n>=2; alpha in (0,1]; symmetric Bernoulli graph with independent upper-triangular entries and zero diagonal
p_ij<=alpha; every expected degree lies between alpha nbar_min and alpha nbar_max
mu=nbar_max/nbar_min; logarithmic sparsity condition with constants depending on nu
normalized adjacency convention; inverse square root is zero at zero degrees

In the multi-season stochastic epidemic framework of Britton and Pugliese, successive epidemic seasons k = 1, 2, ... are driven by an independent and identically distributed sequence of bivariate random vectors (delta_k, tau_k) with joint probability density q(delta, tau) supported on [0, 1] x [0, infinity). The component delta_k in [0, 1] represents seasonal random genetic drift reducing homologous antibody immunity by 1 - delta_k, while tau_k >= 0 represents seasonal transmissibility governing the baseline reproduction number R_0^{(k)} = tau_k.
Sequence of pairs (delta_k, tau_k) is i.i.d.
delta_k in [0, 1] and tau_k >= 0
title: Seasonal Epidemic Genetic Drift and Transmissibility Distribution

DRAFT AUTHOR MODEL CHECK; independent review pending. In the simple C_2*C_3 triangle graph with one a-edge per unordered pair, the forward branching mean is 2p^2+2p^3-2p^4. Replacing every a-edge by two independent parallel Bernoulli(p) bonds changes its connection probability to 2p-p^2 and the branching mean to 4p^2+2p^3-6p^4+2p^5. Its critical equation is 2p^5-6p^4+2p^3+4p^2-1=0, with root in (0.51,0.53), rather than the simple-graph root in (0.63,0.64). These polynomials are checked by 32 and 128 exact local configurations respectively. Kozakova 2008 reports the latter polynomial with Cayley edge multiplicity; that published number must not be transplanted into the simple graph at the same p.

[Lemma 6 (Finite-chaos Stein estimate) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Fix positive integers $q_1,\ldots,q_d$.  Let
$F_{n,a}=I_{q_a}^{(n)}(f_{n,a})$, assume that the kernels are bounded,
and let $C_n=\Cov(F_n)$.  Put
\[
 \Gamma_{n,ab}
 =\ip{DF_{n,a}}{-DL^{-1}F_{n,b}}_{H_n}.
\]
There is a constant $c=c(q_1,\ldots,q_d)<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{a,b=1}^d
 \norm{\Gamma_{n,ab}-C_{n,ab}}_2^2
 \le c\sum_{a,b=1}^d
 \sum_{\substack{1\le r\le q_a\wedge q_b\\
 (r,q_a,q_b)\ne(q_a,q_a,q_a)}}
 \norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,b}}^2.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $Z_n\sim N_d(0,C_n)$, then for every $t\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\E e^{it\cdot F_n}-\E e^{it\cdot Z_n}\right|
 \le\frac{|t|^2}{2}
 \left(
 \sum_{a,b=1}^d
 \norm{\Gamma_{n,ab}-C_{n,ab}}_2^2
 \right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}

[Lemma le:mono-init of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Let $\mathcal{B}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{B}_2 \subsetneq V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} $ be two proper subsets of the cylinder, and let $\o = (\o_1, \o_2, \ldots)$ be a sequence of infinite cylinder walks with prescribed starting sites. For each $i \in \{1, 2\}$ and $k \geq 0$, let $\Phi_k(\mathcal{B}_i)$ denote the cluster obtained from $\mathcal{B}_i$ after the first $k$ walks have been released and settled according to the usual IDLA rule (the $j$-th walk settles at the first site of $\o_j$ outside the current cluster). \[

[Lem localconcentration of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Let $Z\sim N(0, \mathbf{1}_d)$ be a 
$d$-dimensional
standard Gaussian vector. 
Let $\Omega\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a measurable set with 
$\mathbf{P}[Z\in \Omega] \geq \frac{3}{4}$, and let $f: \mathbb{R}^{d}\to \mathbb{R}$ be a
function whose restriction to $\Omega$ is $L$-Lipschitz.
Then
$$
	\mathbf{P}[|f(Z)-\mathrm{med}(f(Z))| > \varepsilon] 
	\leq \mathbf{P}[Z\notin \Omega] + C e^{-c \varepsilon^2/L^2}
$$
for any $\varepsilon>0$, where $C, c>0$ are universal constants.

[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The two estimates on which the critical compactness argument rests are the following.

\textup{(i)} Let $\phi_0>0$ be the normalized local Dirichlet principal eigenfunction. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\sigma_\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
\cA_{\sigma,2,L}\phi_0+(\lambda_0+\varepsilon)\phi_0\ge0\;\hbox{in }(-L,L)
\]
for $0<\sigma<\sigma_\varepsilon$. Consequently $\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,2,L})\le\lambda_0+\varepsilon$.

\textup{(ii)} There exist constants $c_J,C_J>0$ such that
\[
c_J\min\{\eta^2,1\}\le1-\widehat J(\eta)\le C_J\min\{\eta^2,1\}\;\hbox{for all }\eta\in\R.
\]
Consequently, if $\sigma_n\to0$ and $u_n$ are supported in a fixed bounded interval with $\|u_n\|_2\le C$ and $E_{\sigma_n}(u_n)\le C$, then a subsequence converges strongly in $L^2(\R)$ to a function in $H^1(\R)$ supported in the same interval. The estimate is proved directly below from the Fourier symbol. In particular, the proof does not invoke the Sobolev-norm approximation/characterization theorems of \cite{BBM,Brezis02,PonceCV,Ponce}; retaining the zero-extension support is essential for recovering the missing inflow boundary condition in the advective problem.
For every such strongly convergent subsequence, with limit $u$, one also has the sharp lower-semicontinuity estimate
\[
d_J\int_\R |u'(x)|^2\,dx\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}E_{\sigma_n}(u_n).
\]

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2609.00988, 'Covering Projective Height Balls by Subspaces in Rigid Adelic Spaces'] Let $C_2$ be the constant in Lemma~\ref{lem:representatives}.  There are
constants $0<c_8<1$ and $C_8\ge2$, effectively computable from $n, d, r_2, |D_K|, R_K$, with the following property.  Let $F$ be
an $n$-dimensional rigid adelic space over $K$, and write
\[
\lambda_i=\Lambda_i(F),
\qquad
R_i=\frac{1}{8nC_2\lambda_i}
\qquad(1\le i\le n).
\]
If $\mathfrak p\subset\cO_K$ is a nonzero prime ideal, $q=\Nm\mathfrak p$, and
\[
\lambda_n\le c_8,
\qquad
C_8\le q\le c_8\Psi_F(1)^d,
\]
then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $R_i\ge1$ for every $1\le i\le n$;
\item[(ii)] if, for each $1\le i\le n$, the set $S_i=S(R_i,\mathfrak p)$ is chosen as in Lemma~\ref{lem:residue}, then
\[
\prod_{i=1}^n|S_i|>q^{n-1}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 62 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP}(\alpha,q_0)$.
\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$, where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$. Recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, this means there exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_j)^\circ$ (acting in $N_j$ dimensions) such that
    \begin{align} \nonumber 
    &\WERR( (\cA_j)^\circ,\mu)
 \le \epsilon\,,\\
        
   &     q_0(j)
        \equiv \chi_{ (\cA_j)^\circ}(0)
         \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} q_0\,.
    \end{align}
    Let $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be the perturbations of the $( (\cA_j)^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}, which are also $L$-Lipschitz.
    Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} further yields
    \[
        \frac{1}{N} \bbE \Big[\| (\cA_j)^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) 
        	- \cA_j(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2\Big]
        \le \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2}\,.
    \]
Thus Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx} implies that for $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$ and $C_2(\alpha,L)$ given therein,
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_j,(\cA_j)^\circ)
	\le 
	\bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) \cdot \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2} + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j}
        \bigg\}^{1/2} 
        \le \epsilon \]
    where the last inequality holds if $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$ (consistent with our assumptions), and $j$ sufficiently large depending on $q_0,\epsilon,L$. Hence, by omitting finitely many $j$, we can assume it holds for all $j$ that
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\cA_j,\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le 2\epsilon\,,
    \eeq
By passing to a further subsequence of the $j$'s, we can assume that for all $j$ we have 
    \[
         \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \mu^\Ising\Big)
        \bigg\}
         \le 3\epsilon
    \]
for some fixed $\mu^\Ising \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$.
    By passing to a further subsequence, we can assume (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}) that $\chi_{\cA_j}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, both pointwise and in $L^1$.
    Since Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} ensures 
    \[
        \chi_{\cA_j}(0) = \chi_{\cA^\circ_j}(0) = q_0(j)\,,
    \]
    by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.q0.limit} we have $\chi(0) = q_0$.

We now apply Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} to the sequence $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ where, treating $\epsilon$ as a function of $L$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly, the hypothesis \eqref{e:BOGP-hardness-main-hypothesis} holds by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.hardness.hypothesis}.
    Then, for some $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon)$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly as $\epsilon\rightarrow 0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} provides controls $(q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conclusions of that theorem, where all $o_L(1)$ error terms are replaced by $\tilde\epsilon$. We assume without loss that $\tilde{\epsilon}\le1$. 
    We will now verify that for $C(L)$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main},
    \beq
        
         (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) 
         \in \Adm^{\BOGP}\Big(
         \alpha,q_0;
         \tilde C = \max\{C(L),L^2\}, \tilde\epsilon 
         \Big)\,.
    \eeq
    Indeed, we verify each of the conditions from Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} specifying the $\Adm^{\BOGP}$ class:
    \begin{itemize}
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-Lip}
    implies condition~\ref{it:1.1bogp};

\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-diffusivity}
    implies condition~\ref{it:2.1}; 

\item We have $p(q_0) = 0$ because we defined $\chi(0) = q_0$.

body: A graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two parts X and Y with every edge joining X to Y - equivalently, it contains no odd cycle (Konig). A matching is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges; it saturates a set S if every vertex of S is an endpoint of a matching edge, and it is perfect if it saturates every vertex. In a bipartite graph, Hall's marriage condition - |N(S)| >= |S| for every subset S of X, where N(S) is the neighborhood - is exactly the condition under which X can be saturated by a matching.
title: Bipartite Graph and Matching

body: In the mathematical discipline of graph theory, Menger's theorem says that in a finite graph, the size of a minimum cut set is equal to the maximum number of disjoint paths that can be found between any pair of vertices. Proved by Karl Menger in 1927, it characterizes the connectivity of a graph. It is generalized by the max-flow min-cut theorem, which is a weighted, edge version, and which in turn is a special case of the strong duality theorem for linear programs.
title: Menger's theorem

body:
[Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, and let $\bx(q_d)$ be as defined by
\eqref{e:x.q.mean}. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\bigg|
    \frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}-q_{\min\{d,\ell\}}
    \bigg|\ge
    \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\bigg) 
    \le \exp(-N^{0.1})\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
This follows easily from gaussian Lipschitz concentration (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}).
Indeed note that $\|\cA(\bG,  \bg^\aux)\|_2\leq N^{1/2}$ almost surely, while by definition $\bx(q_d)$
is an $L$-Lipschitz function of the gaussian vector $(\bG(q_d),\bg^\aux(q_d))$. It follows that for $\ell \le d$, the normalized inner product
    \[\frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}\]
is an 
 $O(LN^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function of 
    \[\Big(\bG(q_\ell),
    \bg^\aux(q_\ell),
    \bG(q_d) - \bG(q_\ell),\bg^\aux(q_d) - \bg^\aux(q_\ell)\Big)\,.\]
 Therefore it concentrates around its mean by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}, which gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Lemma stability of arXiv:2603.15323, '\Large \bf Small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums'] {[vB87]}
Let $D$ be a bounded $C^{1,1}$ open set in ${\mathbb R}^{d}$ with characteristic $(R_0, \Lambda_0)$ and define for $0\leq q <R_{0}$,
$$
D_{q}=\{x\in D : \delta_{D}(x)>q\}.
$$
Then
$$
\left(\frac{R_{0}-q}{R_{0}}\right)^{d-1}|\partial D|\leq |\partial D_{q}| \leq \left(\frac{R_{0}}{R_{0}-q}\right)^{d-1}|\partial D|,
\quad 0\leq q < R_{0}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma stability of arXiv:2603.15323

body:
[Lemma forward estimate of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] Let $k \geq 0$ and let $v$ be a vertex that can create a forward $d$-dimensional simplex with a $(d-1)$-simplex $\sigma_k$ that is being explored at Step $k$. Then, given $\mathcal{X}_{k-1}$, the probability that $\sigma_k \cup \{v\}$ appears at Step $k$ is lower bounded by
\[  \tag{3.2.3}
p_k^F := \left( 1 - (k-1) \frac{\lambda}{n} - \sum_{\ell = 1}^{d-1} \sum_{\rho \subseteq \sigma_k, \dim(\rho) = \ell-1} \deg_{\ell-1, d-1}^{\mathcal{X}_{k-1}} (\rho)  p_{d, \ell}  \right) \left( \frac{\lambda}{n} + o(1) \right).
\]
In particular, if the given MRSC model is the Linial-Meshulam model, the probability is exactly $\lambda/n + o(1)$.

body:
[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2506.13347, 'Ergodic theorem for the differential equations with interaction'] Assume that for equation with Lipschitz coefficient $a: \mathbb{R} \times \mathfrak M_{0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x\left(u,t\right)=a\left(x(u, t), \mu_{t}\right) d t \\
x(u, 0)=u \in \mathbb{R}, \\
\mu_{t}=\mu_{0} \circ x(\cdot, t)^{-1}
\end{array}\right.
$$
there exists a set $A$ of invariant initial measures,
that is $A=\left\{\mu \in \mathfrak M_{0}: \Phi_{t}(\mu)=\mu, \ t \geq 0\right\}$.
Then the measure $\varkappa$ on $\mathfrak M_{0}$ of the form
$$
\varkappa=\sum_{k=1}^{N} \delta \mu_{k} \cdot p_{k}, \quad \mu_{k} \in A
$$
is invariant with respect to $\Phi_{t}$ :
$$
\varkappa \circ \Phi_{t}^{-1}=\varkappa .
$$

[Proposition prop:geom of arXiv:2604.23791, 'Finite-sample Borel--Cantelli inequalities under mixing conditions'] Suppose $\varphi(n)\le C\rho^{n}$ and $p:=\inf_{k}\mathbb{P}(A_{k})>0$. Choose an
integer $L_{0}\ge0$ with $C\rho^{L_{0}+1}\le p/2$. Then for every
$N\ge1$,
\[
  \mathbb{P}\Bigl(\,\bigcup_{k=1}^{N}A_{k}\,\Bigr)
  \;\ge\; 1-\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{S_{N}}{2(L_{0}+1)}\Bigr)
  \;\ge\; 1-\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{pN}{2(L_{0}+1)}\Bigr).
\]

[Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(x_n,y_n,x,y\in D([0,\infty),\bR)\).
Assume the following:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(x_n\to x\) on \(D([0,\infty),\bR)\) as \(n\to\infty\),
  \item \(y_n\) and \(y\) are non-decreasing, with
  \[
  y(0)=0,
  \quad
  y_n(\infty)=y(\infty)=\infty,
  \]
  \item \(y\) is strictly increasing,
  \item there exists a dense subset \(D\subset[0,\infty)\) such that
  \[
  y_n(u)\to y(u)
  \quad (n\to\infty)
  \]
  for every \(u\in D\).
\end{enumerate}
Then, for every \(t\ge0\) such that \(x\) is continuous at \(y^{-1}(t)\), we have
\begin{align}
x_n(y_n^{-1}(t))\longrightarrow x(y^{-1}(t))
\quad (n\to\infty),

\end{align}
where \(y_n^{-1}\) and \(y^{-1}\) denote the right-continuous inverses. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 17 of arXiv:2605.23659

[Proposition 38 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] In the setting of the preceding corollary, let
\(w=(w^1,\ldots,w^m)\) be holomorphic coordinates centered at
\(q\), and let \(\tau_i\searrow0\) realize a tangent space at \(\xi\).
After passing to a further subsequence realizing the same tangent space,
there is a
choice of the product isometry in \eqref{ti:eq:rigid-product} and a
matrix \(L\in\mathrm{GL}(m,\C)\), depending on the chosen tangent-space
realization and on \(w\) but independent of \(i\), such that
\begin{equation}
 L\!\left(\tau_i^{-1/2}w\circ\pi\right)
 \longrightarrow \operatorname{pr}_{\C^m}
\end{equation}
smoothly on every compact regular convergence chart.  The normalization
is complex linear and contains no translation.  Write
\(F_q:=\pi^{-1}(q)\).  Wherever the coordinate chart is defined,
\begin{equation}
 (w\circ\pi)^{-1}(0)=F_q,
 \qquad
 Z'=\operatorname{pr}_{\C^m}^{-1}(0)_{\rm red}.
\end{equation}

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Two equations with identical classical solutions can have different weak solutions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.
Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0
Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter
Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1

Result: The energy-minimising path between two points concentrates on paths of small total resistance, i.e. on near-geodesics of the discrete metric with edge weights e^{beta h}; this is the Liouville first passage percolation metric, whose scaling limit (the LQG metric) exists for beta below the critical value by Ding-Dubedat-Dunlap-Falconet and Gwynne-Miller. Tightness of P is then plausible via geodesic tightness in that metric, but P is not a geodesic: the current spreads over many paths and the minimiser of the quadratic energy is a flow, not a path; the notes' 'path' is the sampled path of the current. Its scaling limit would be a random path sampled from the limiting current, which requires the continuum current on LQG, an object not yet constructed. I record the reduction: existence of the limit of P is equivalent to existence of the continuum electrical current between boundary points on the LQG surface. Obstruction: No continuum electrical current on LQG has been constructed; the path is a functional of it.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0015-scaling-limit-of-the-current-minimising-path-in-the-dgff-network
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved
title: Attempt on Scaling limit of the current-minimising path in the DGFF network

At each fixed finite t for sparse critical parking on Z^d, d>=3, the common-Abel full-space potential V_t=lim_{a->1}G_a*(eta-(A_t-H_t)) exists in L2 and U_t-E U_t=V_t+M_t, where M_t is the C17 Green instruction martingale. The odometer mean is a harmonic mode; the two components are not asserted independent. In d4 the difference is well-defined although raw individual charge potentials diverge. Assumptions: Bounded sparse iid source law, 0<p<1/2; finite t; d>=3; Full-space discrete-time SRW, (I-P)G=delta; common Abel parameter; Source finite propagation gives finite-dependent centered U_t; C17 L2 Green instruction martingale. Limitation: No time-uniform potential variance, Gaussian law or independence; no nearest-distance conclusion. Novelty: KNOWN stationary Poisson/resolvent method; UNCHECKED exact parking decomposition. Status: proof (unaudited). The model is discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous parking on Z^d with stationary capacity-one holes; A_t(x) is the active-particle count and H_t(x) the unfilled-hole indicator. In the sparse law eta(x) is initially +1 and -1 each with probability p, and zero otherwise, independently across sites. In this card V_t denotes the charge-difference potential, not the eligible-site indicator V_t in C23; these are separate local notations. No audit has been completed for this exact version. U_t(y) counts departures through time t, rho_j(y) is the destination of its jth used instruction, P is the nearest-neighbor averaging operator, G_a=sum_{n>=0}a^n p_n, and M_t(x)=L2-lim_{a->1}sum_y sum_{j<=U_t(y)}[G_a(rho_j(y)-x)-(P G_a)(y-x)].
Bounded sparse iid source law, 0<p<1/2; finite t; d>=3
Full-space discrete-time SRW, (I-P)G=delta; common Abel parameter

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:098746b1e0dab25f3f7060ed4d8184a8ee644d9b374a0482f67f64ee375ca5d8","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/09/098746b1e0dab25f3f7060ed4d8184a8ee644d9b374a0482f67f64ee375ca5d8.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:003ee7cd411bd14e46e167b8c6d8c2748dacb1466880217907ba41819bb91206","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c25","bundle_id":"population.i0005-final-exploration-energy-and-charge-007","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and interacting particle systems","draft":"w661/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:parking-centered-odometer-common-abel-charge-difference-decomposition-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C25 v1: centered odometer and a common Abel charge potential

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN stationary Poisson/resolvent
method; UNCHECKED this exact parking Abel decomposition. The terms are
not assumed independent and no time-uniform variance bound follows.

For the sparse critical source process on Z^d, d>=3, 0<p<1/2, fix a
finite horizon t. Let S_t=A_t-H_t, m_t=E U_t(0), and

    N_t(x)=sum_y sum_{j<=U_t(y)}
                  [1{rho_j(y)=x}-p_1(x-y)].

This is accumulated arrival instruction noise. For 0<a<1 let
G_a(x)=sum_{n>=0}a^n p_n(x), the full-space discrete-time Abel Green
kernel. The limit

    V_t(x)=L2-lim_{a->1} [G_a*(eta-S_t)](x)

exists, and the exact centered identity is

    U_t(x)-m_t=V_t(x)+M_t(x),

where M_t is C17's deterministic Green-potential instruction martingale
with covariance m_t[2G(z-x)-1{x=z}]. All convolutions use the same full-space
SRW convention (I-P)G=delta. In d4 the raw eta and S_t potentials separately
have divergent variance (C24); their difference is regularized together.
The mean m_t is a spatially constant harmonic mode and cannot be recovered
by inverting I-P on mean-zero charges.

## 1. Exact finite-Abel algebra

Source conservation (19) and the definition of N_t give

    S_t=eta+(P-I)U_t+N_t,
    eta-S_t=(I-P)U_t-N_t.

At fixed t under the bounded sparse law, all local counts have a deterministic
finite bound. G_a is in l1, with total mass 1/(1-a), so these convolutions
are well-defined absolutely at a<1 and commute with P. Therefore

    G_a*(eta-S_t)=G_a*(I-P)(U_t-m_t)-G_a*N_t.

The constant was removed because (I-P)m_t=0. Expanding the arrival noise
and using symmetry of G_a shows

    (G_a*N_t)(x)=sum_y sum_{j<=U_t(y)}
                  [G_a(rho_j(y)-x)-(P G_a)(y-x)]
                =M_t^a(x).

The rearrangement is legitimate: at fixed t U_t(y) is uniformly bounded,
and the sum of neighbor Green weights is finite at a<1. C17 proves
M_t^a converges in L2 to M_t for d>=3.

## 2. Resolvent filter converges to the centered identity

Set Z_t=U_t-m_t. The field Z_t is stationary, square-integrable and
finite-dependent by source finite propagation from iid bounded initial
data and independent local motion randomness. Its covariance therefore
has finite support and an absolutely continuous spectral measure; in
particular there is no atom at frequency zero.

The SRW Fourier multiplier is lambda(theta)=d^(-1)sum_i cos(theta_i).
The filter G_a*(I-P) has multiplier

    b_a(theta)=(1-lambda)/(1-a lambda).

For lambda>=0, 0<=b_a<=1; for lambda<0 it is bounded by two.
At every frequency with lambda!=1 it tends to one as a tends to one.
The only frequency lambda=1 is zero, which has no spectral atom for Z_t.
Dominated convergence against its finite spectral measure yields

    G_a*(I-P)Z_t -> Z_t in L2.

Combining this with Step 1 and C17 gives convergence of the charge-difference
potential and the claimed identity. This also proves why centering is
required: b_a(0)=0 at every a and the mean mode is annihilated.

## 3. Scope of cancellation

The difference eta-S_t is a stationary current divergence; covariance
reindexing as in C19 shows its susceptibility is zero. This is consistent
with the existence of its potential even when the two individual raw
charge potentials diverge. It is not legitimate to subtract two separately
defined infinite-variance limits; the same Abel parameter regularizes their
difference before passing to the limit.

Both V_t and M_t depend on the same routing and final configuration.
No independence between them is claimed. The identity supplies a correct
potential decomposition at each finite time, not a bound on V_t as time
grows, a Gaussian approximation, or a conditional hole-influence estimate.
The remaining d4 nearest-distance problem still requires spatial control.

Primary source: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis arXiv:2609.02820v1, (19), Lemma 4.3
and finite propagation. C17 supplies the Abel instruction martingale;

body: Two Latin squares of order n are orthogonal if superimposing them produces each of the n^2 ordered pairs of symbols exactly once; a family is a set of MOLS if every pair in it is orthogonal, and N(n) denotes the maximum size of such a family. For every n >= 2, N(n) <= n - 1, with equality whenever n is a prime power via the finite-field construction L_a(i, j) = a i + j over F_n for nonzero a. N(1) is infinite by convention, and N(2) = N(6) = 1.
title: Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares (MOLS)

[Corollary 16 (Integrated Davies trick - normalized) of arXiv:2609.01098, 'Gaussian upper bounds for averaged heat semigroups on graphs'] For any $q\in[1,\infty]$, denote by $q'$ its H\"older conjugate and let $A,B\subset X$, and $I\subset \RR$. Then, for any $q$-norm with respect to any measure on $X$, we have 
\begin{multline*}
\left(
\fint_I \tvert{P_{2\tau}}_{A,B,q',q}\drm \tau 
\right)^\frac{2}{q}
\\
\leq 
\inf_{\omega\in\ell^\infty(X)}
\sup_{A}\euler^{-\omega}
\sup_{B}\euler^{\omega}
\left(
\fint_I
\tvert{P_\tau^\omega}_{A,A,2,q}^q
\drm \tau
\right)^\frac{1}{q}
\left(
\fint_I
\tvert{P_\tau^{-\omega}}_{B,B,2,q}^q
\drm \tau
\right)^\frac{1}{q}.
\end{multline*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Integrated Davies trick - normalized
Uniformly Parabolic Operator in Nondivergence Form

[Dfn 3. dfn: metric on frakMtau of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The metrics $d_{\mathfrak{M}_{c}}^{\tau}$ and $d_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\tau}$}]  
  Let $\tau$ be a functor on $\mathfrak{M}$.
  For $\mathcal{S}=(S,d^{S}, \rho_{S}, a_{S}), \mathcal{T}=(T, d^{T}, \rho_{T}, a_{T}) \in \mathfrak{M}(\tau)$,
  we define
  \begin{equation} 
    d_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\tau} (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{T})
    \coloneqq
    \inf_{f, g, M}
    \left\{
      \lHausdMet{M}{\rho_{M}} \bigl( f(S), g(T) \bigr) 
      \vee  
      d_{\tau}^{M,\rho_{M}} \bigl( \tau_{f}(a_{S}), \tau_{g}(a_{T}) \bigr)  
    \right\},
  \end{equation}
  where the infimum is taken 
  over all $(M, d^{M}, \rho_{M}) \in \mathfrak{M}$ 
  and root-and-distance-preserving maps $f : S \to M$ and $g : T \to M$.
  For a functor $\tau$ on $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$,
  we define $d_{\mathfrak{M}_{c}}^{\tau}$ similarly.
title: Dfn 3. dfn: metric on frakMtau of arXiv:2412.08236

body: Let (mu_n) be a sequence of probability measures on a topological space X equipped with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let (a_n) be a sequence of positive reals with a_n tending to infinity (the speed). A function I: X -> [0, infinity] is a rate function if it is lower semicontinuous; it is a good rate function if in addition every sublevel set {x in X : I(x) <= alpha}, alpha < infinity, is compact. The sequence (mu_n) satisfies a large-deviation principle with speed a_n and rate function I if, for every Borel set B, -inf_{x in int(B)} I(x) <= liminf_n (1/a_n) log mu_n(B) <= limsup_n (1/a_n) log mu_n(B) <= -inf_{x in cl(B)} I(x), where int(B) and cl(B) denote the interior and closure of B. [Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications]
title: Large-Deviation Principle and Rate Function

[Definition 9 (Weak sub-solution) of arXiv:2608.26834, 'Small-time annealed large deviations principle for one-dimensional diffusions in a random '] A nonnegative function $u$ on $(0,S)\times D$ is called a bounded weak sub-solution  of the differential equation
		\begin{equation}
			\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}={\mathcal L}_W u
		\end{equation}
		if
		\[
		u\in L^\infty((0,S)\times D) \cap L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,S);H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)),
		\]
		and, for every nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^1((0,S);H_0^1(D)\cap L^\infty(D))$, one has
		\begin{equation*}
			-\int_0^S\!\int_Du\,\partial_s\varphi\,\dd \mu_W\dd s
			+\int_0^S\mathcal E_W(u(s),\varphi(s))\,\dd s\le0.
		\end{equation*}
		If equality holds for all such $\varphi$, then $u$ is called a weak solution.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: A finite-horizon input coupling suggests a cubic collision scale. Fix k tagged servers. Jobs arrive at rate Lambda=lambda*n/k and choose a uniform k-subset. If N is the number of tagged servers hit by an arrival, E[N(N-1)]=k*(k-1)*k*(k-1)/(n*(n-1)). Remove arrivals that hit at least two tagged queues and restore their lost marginal rates by independent Poisson streams. A union bound on removed events and added events is at most (3/2)*Lambda*T*E[N(N-1)], hence at most 3*lambda*T*k*(k-1)^2/(2*(n-1)). The resulting streams are independent with the correct marginal rates. With independent task marks and queues initially empty, this also bounds total variation of their workload paths on [0,T]. Extending the credited source coupling to stationary starts gives TV<=2*k*r(T)+3*lambda*T*k*(k-1)^2/(2*(n-1)), where r(T) is the stationary marginal emptying tail. With independent exponential service of rate mu>lambda, a stopped generator calculation gives r(T)<=(1+sqrt(lambda/mu))*exp(-(sqrt(mu)-sqrt(lambda))^2*T). Taking T=2*log(n)/(sqrt(mu)-sqrt(lambda))^2 gives sufficient k=o((n/log(n))^(1/3)). A conditional polynomial tail r(T)<=C*T^(-p) gives sufficient exponent p/(3*p+1). Check: The hypergeometric factorial moment follows by summing ordered pairs of tagged-server indicators. On N>=2, both 1<=N(N-1)/2 and N<=N(N-1), giving the factor 3/2. Small subset enumeration checks the moment exactly. Separate exact checks cover 77 hypergeometric/restoration cases, 81 generator identities, nine geometric exponential moments and five polynomial balancing identities. The complete packet explicitly checks stationary coupling, marginal rate restoration, PASTA and heavy-traffic limits; these are author checks, not independent review. Obstruction: Partial exponential-service sufficient regime only. No optimal threshold, boundary k of order n^(1/3), general-service improvement, correlated-mark result, uniform heavy-traffic result or novelty certification. The basic source coupling is credited.

[Definition def:FktdAJs of arXiv:2609.02588, 'Ramsey-type results for Maker-Breaker games'] Let $k,t,d,s,r$ be positive integers with $t\geq d \geq 2$ and $k\geq r$,
let $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \binom{[t]\setminus \{1\}}{d-1}$
and $\mathcal{K}\in \binom{[t]\setminus \{1\}}{d-1} \setminus \mathcal{A}$.
We define $\mathcal{F}_s(k,t,d,\mathcal{A},\mathcal{K},r)$ to be the family of all 
$d$-uniform hypergraphs
$\mathcal{H}$ that satisfy the following property:
There exists a partition of the vertex set $V(\mathcal{H}) = V_1\cup \ldots \cup V_t$
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $|V_i| = k$ for every $i\in [t]$,
\item[(ii)] $|e\cap V_i| \leq 1$ for every $i\in [t]$ and $e\in E(\mathcal{H})$,
\item[(iii)] for every $i\in [t]$, every vertex $v\in V_i$, 
every index set $J\in \binom{[t]\setminus [i]}{d-1}$ and every choice of sets
$A_j\in \binom{V_j}{s}$ for $j\in J$, we have 
$e_{\mathcal{H}}\big( \{v\}\cup \bigcup_{j\in J} A_j\big) \neq 0$,
\item[(iv)] for every $v\in V_1$ and every $J\in \mathcal{A}$ we have 
	$\mathcal{H}_v\big[ \bigcup_{j\in J} V_j \big] \cong H_{k,d-1,d-1}$,
\item[(v)] there exists a set $X_1 \in \binom{V_1}{r}$ such that 
	 $\mathcal{H}_v\big[ \bigcup_{j\in \mathcal{K}} V_j \big] \cong H_{k,d-1,d-1}$ for every $v\in X_1$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition def:FktdAJs of arXiv:2609.02588

[Prop pr.Topo of arXiv:2411.13099, 'Long time behavior of killed Feynman-Kac semigroups with singular Schr{ö}dinger potentials'] Let $(L_t,t\ge 0)$ be a purely jump Lévy process over $\mathscr R^d$ such that its  Lévy measure $\nu$ has full topological support over $\mathscr R_0^d$, i.e. for all $y\in \mathscr R^d_0$ and all $r\in (0,|y|)$, $\nu(B(y,r))>0$, and such that for some $\beta >0$, 
 $$\int_{|u|\le 1}|u|^\beta \nu(du)<+\infty.$$  Let $\mathscr O$ be a subdomain of $\mathscr R^d$. 
 Let  $T>0$ and $x,z\in \mathscr O$. Then,  for all $\epsilon>0$, 
 \begin{equation}
 \mathbb P_x[|L_T-z|<\epsilon, T<\sigma _{\mathscr O}]>0,
 \end{equation}
 where $\sigma_{\mathscr O}:=\inf\{t\ge 0, L_t\notin \mathscr O\}$. 
 In addition, if $\mathscr R^d\setminus \overline{\mathscr O}$ is nonempty, for all $x\in \mathscr O$, $\mathbb P_x[\sigma_{\mathscr O}<+\infty ]>0$.
title: Prop pr.Topo of arXiv:2411.13099

\[

\]

Positive-axis continuation and nonnegative coefficients give summability below the root; a noncanceled E-zero pole gives divergence at and above it. This is the exact cutoff of a sufficient raw-profile METHOD, not the actual good/bad transition. It does not settle the conjectured all-good interval down to 4/5 or the low-drift side, and no novelty is asserted.

[Corollary Constant alternating regret for polyhedral OLO of arXiv:2608.24731, 'Optimal Alternating Regret for Online Learning and Games\thanks{Authors are alphabetically'] \label[corollary]{cor:polytope}
Let $\mathcal X=\operatorname{conv}\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_N\}$ be a  polytope. Consider  linear losses $f_t(\boldsymbol{x})=\langle \boldsymbol{c}_t,\boldsymbol{x}\rangle$, with $f_t(\boldsymbol{x})\in[-1,1]$ for every $\boldsymbol{x}\in\+X$. Running (alg:main of the paper) with $\mu$ being the uniform distribution on $\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_N\}$ gives
\[
  \max_{\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathcal X}\operatorname{Reg}_{\mathrm{Alt}}^T(\boldsymbol{u})\le8\log N.
\]
In particular, for $\mathcal X=\Delta_d$ and $\boldsymbol{c}_t\in[-1,1]^d$, (alg:main of the paper) coincides with (alg:variance hedge of the paper) and recovers the bound $8\log d$.

[Proposition 29 ({\bf The Interval of Integers Principle}) of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $X\rightarrow X/G$ is an HKG cover. For each integer $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ let the pair $(\l_{j,0},\l_{j,-1})\in (\mathbb N\cup\{0\})\times\llbracket0,m-1\rrbracket$ be such that 
$$\Big\lfloor\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\Big\rfloor=m\l_{j,0}+\l_{j,-1};$$
e.g., $(\l_{0,0},\l_{0,-1})\in (\mathbb N\cup\{0\})\times\llbracket0,m-1\rrbracket$ is such that $\lfloor\frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor=m\l_{0,0}+\l_{0,-1}$. Let $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$ and let the pair $(\q_{s,b},\r_{s,b})\in \mathbb Z\times\llbracket0,m-1\rrbracket$ be such that $\delta_s(b-1)-\delta_s(b)=m\q_{s,b}+\r_{s,b}$.  Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} If either $a=[0]_m$ with $\delta_s(b)\ge 1$ (i.e., with $b\le p^s-2$) or $a\neq [0]_m$, then we have identities
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}\mu_X(a,b)=&\q_{s,b}+\Big\lfloor\frac{\delta_s(b)-1+\r_{-a}+\r_{s,b}}{m}\Big\rfloor-\Big\lfloor\frac{\delta_s(b)-1+\r_{-a}}{m}\Big\rfloor\\
=&\begin{cases}\q_{s,b}+1\quad\;\textup{if}\quad \r_{\delta_s(b)-1+\r_{-a}}+\r_{s,b}\ge m\\
\q_{s,b}\quad\quad\quad\textup{if}\quad \r_{\delta_s(b)-1+\r_{-a}}+\r_{s,b}<m.\end{cases}
\end{split}
\end{equation}
In particular, we have $\mu_X(a,b)=\q_{s,b}+1$ if and only if $\r_{s,b}\neq 0$ (i.e., $\r_{s,b}\in\llbracket1,m-1\rrbracket$) and $a\in [\delta_s(b)]_m+\{[i]_m|i\in\llbracket0,\r_{s,b}-1\rrbracket\}$.

{\bf (2)} We have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\q_{s,p^s-1}=\Big\lfloor\frac{\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1}{m}\Big\rfloor=\begin{cases}\l_{0,0}+1\quad\textup{if}\quad\l_{0,-1}=m-1\\
\l_{0,0}\quad\quad\;\;\,\textup{if}\quad \l_{0,-1}\in\llbracket0,m-2\rrbracket,\end{cases}
\end{equation*} 
$\r_{s,p^s-1}=\Big\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\Big\rfloor+1-m\Big\lfloor\frac{\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1}{m}\Big\rfloor$, and
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}\mu_X([0]_m,p^s-1)=\q_{s,p^s-1}+\Big\lfloor\frac{\delta_s(p^s-1)-1+\r_{s,p^s-1}}{m}\Big\rfloor-1-\Big\lfloor\frac{\delta_s(p^s-1)-1}{m}\Big\rfloor\\
=\l_{0,0}=\begin{cases}\q_{s,p^s-1}\quad\quad\quad\textup{if}\quad \r_{s,p^s-1}\ge 1\\
\q_{s,p^s-1}-1\quad\;\textup{if}\quad \r_{s,p^s-1}=0\end{cases}=\begin{cases}\Big\lfloor\frac{\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1}{m}\Big\rfloor\quad\quad\quad\;\;\textup{if}\quad m\nmid \lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1\\
\Big\lfloor\frac{\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1}{m}\Big\rfloor-1\quad\;\;\;\textup{if}\quad m\mid\lfloor \frac{l_1}{p}\rfloor+1.\end{cases}
\end{split}
\end{equation}

{\bf (3)} For each $a\in C_m$ we have inequalities 
$$\mu_X([0]_m,p^s-1)\le\mu_X(a,p^s-1)\le \mu_X([0]_m,p^s-1)+1.$$

{\bf (4)} For each pair $(a_1,a_2)\in C_m^2$ and every $b\in\llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$ we have inequalities $0\le |\mu_X(a_1,b)-\mu_X(a_2,b)|\le 1$.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} Let $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$. We assume that $b\in A_{s;j}$; so $p^j\mid b$ but $p^{j+1}\nmid b$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (5.a)} We have identities
$$\q_{s,b}=\begin{cases}\l_{j,0}+1\quad\quad\textup{if}\quad\l_{j,-1}=m-1\quad\textup{and}\quad \r_{s,b}=0\\
\l_{j,0}\quad\quad\quad\;\;\,\textup{if}\quad\l_{j,-1}=m-1\quad\textup{and}\quad \r_{s,b}>0\\
\l_{j,0}\quad\quad\quad\;\;\,\textup{if}\quad \l_{j,-1}\in\llbracket0,m-2\rrbracket.\end{cases}$$

\noindent
{\bf (5.b)} If $j=0$ we assume that $b\neq p^s-1$. Then for each $a\in C_m$ we have inequalities 
$$\l_{j,0}\le \q_{s,b}\le\mu_X(a,b)\le \l_{j,0}+1\le\q_{s,b}+1.$$

\noindent
{\bf (5.c)} If $\l_{j,-1}=m-1$, $\r_{s,b}=0$, and for $j=0$ we have $b\neq p^s-1$, then $\mu_X(a,b)=\q_{s,b}=\l_{j,0}+1$.

\noindent
{\bf (5.d)} There exists a uniquely determined subset $\mathbb J_{X;j}$ of $C_m\times A_{s;j}$ such that 
$$\mu_X(a,b)=\begin{cases}\l_{j,0}+1\quad\;\textup{if}\quad (a,b)\in\mathbb J_{X;j}\\
\l_{j,0}\quad\quad\quad\textup{if}\quad (a,b)\in(C_m\times A_{s;j})\setminus\mathbb J_{X;j}.\end{cases}$$

{\bf (6)} Let $\mathbb J_X:=\sqcup_{j=0}^{s-1}\mathbb J_{X;j}$. We have an identity

[Lem 18 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In the setting of Proposition~\ref{p:polytope.bd.local}, 
we can construct a family of half-spaces $(\tilde{H}_j : j\in[\tilde{n}])$
such that for $\delta_0>0$ small enough, we have

        P\supseteq 
        \tilde{P}_\mu &\equiv \cD_\mu \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^{\tilde n} \tilde H_j 
        \supseteq S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon']\,, \quad \text{and} \\
        
        	\emptyset \ne 
        \tilde{P}_{\mu'} &\equiv \cD_{\mu'} \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^{\tilde n} \tilde H_j 
        \subseteq 
        S_\star\bigg(\lambda',\mu';
        	\frac\epsilon5,\frac\epsilon2-\delta_0
        	\bigg)\,.
    \end{align}
for all $(\lambda',\mu') \in B_{\delta_0}(\lambda,\mu)$. 

\begin{proof}Let $n = C(\lambda,\mu)$. Let $(H_j:j\in[n])$ be a collection of closed half-spaces of $\bbR^{3r+s}$ such that
	\[
        K_1=S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon']
        \subseteq P
        \equiv \cD_\mu \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^n H_j
        \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        	\frac\epsilon5,\frac\epsilon2\bigg)
        =K_2\,.\]
Abbreviate $u_\mu\equiv (0^{3r},\mu)$, and recall from \eqref{e:D.mu.affine.closure} that the affine space $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ is defined by the constraint $(\YY,u_\mu)=1$. In the above definition of $P$, we can assume without loss that none of the $H_j$ have normal vector parallel to $u_\mu$: such $H_j$ are redundant because of the intersection with $\cD_\mu$. 

Recall that the function $f$ from \eqref{e:f.strictly.convex.surplus.relaxation}
is strictly convex on $\cD_\mu$.
We also have
	\[
	P\subseteq K_2
	=\bigg\{\YY \in \cD_\mu : f(\YY;\lambda,\mu) \le 	
	\frac\epsilon2
		\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The strict convexity of $f$ implies that the set 
    \[
        \cQ \equiv \bigg\{
        	\YY \in P : f(\YY;\lambda,\mu) = \frac\epsilon2
		\bigg\}
    \]
must be a subset of the extreme points of $P$ (the points that cannot be written as a convex combination of two other points in $P$). Therefore, $\cQ$ is a discrete set.
    Moreover, Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps} implies
    \[
        S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] \subseteq
        \bigg\{\YY \in P : f(\YY;\lambda,\mu) \le 
        	\frac\epsilon3
        	\bigg\}\,,
    \]
and thus $\cQ \cap S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon'] = \emptyset$. Enumerate the points of $\cQ$ as $\YY_1,\ldots,\YY_{\hat{n}}$, and for each $j\in[\hat{n}]$ let $\hat{H}_j$ be a closed half-space in $\R^{3r+s}$ whose interior contains $K_1$, and which does not contain $\YY_j$. We then construct the collection $(\tilde H_j : j\in[\tilde{n}])$ by appending these half-spaces to $(H_j:j\in[n])$, so that $\tilde{n}=n+\hat{n}$. Note that $\hat{H}_j$ strictly separates $\YY_j\in\cD_\mu$ from $K_1\subseteq\cD_\mu$, so the normal vector of $\hat{H}_j$ cannot be parallel to $u_\mu$. 

Recall from \eqref{e:polytope-tilde1} and \eqref{e:polytope-tilde2}
that we denote 
	\[
	\tilde{P}_{\mu'}
	\equiv \cD_{\mu'} \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^{\tilde{n}} \tilde{H}_j\,.
	\]
From the above construction combined with Lemma~\ref{l:p.polytope.bd.local.aux}, we have
	\[
	K_1\subseteq \tilde{P}_\mu \subseteq P\setminus\cQ
	\subseteq P
	\subseteq K_2
	\subseteq \cD_\mu
	\cap \bigg[0,\frac{8}{\iota_0}\bigg]^{3r+s}
	 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_\mu
	 \cap \bigg[0,\frac{8}{\iota_0}\bigg]^{3r+s}\,.

If $\YY\in \mathrm{int}(\tilde{P}_\mu;\mathcal{F}_\mu)$, then for all $\YY'$ orthogonal to $u_\mu$ with $\|\YY'\|$ small enough, we must have $\YY+\YY' \in\tilde{P}_\mu$. body: In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle. The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group which can be computed as isomorphic to the group where corresponds to an even number of twists, and to an odd number.
title: Cohomology

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph of maximal degree at most $\Delta$, and for each $(u,v)\in E$ we are given constants $\beta_{uv}$ where $|\beta_{uv}|\leq\beta$ for all edges. Fix an arbitrary external field $h=(h_u)_{u\in V}$, an arbitrary subset $A\subset V$ and configuration $\tau\in\{0,1\}^A$. Then whenever $\beta\leq\frac{1}{\Delta}$, the measure $\mu_{\beta,h}$ defined on $\{0,1\}^{V\setminus A}$ via
$$
\mu_{\beta,h}(\sigma)\propto\exp(\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\beta_{uv}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{u\in V\setminus A}h_u\sigma_u),\quad\forall\sigma\in\{0,1\}^V:\sigma|_A=\tau
$$satisfies approximate tensorization of variance and approximate tensorization of entropy with constant 2.

[Defn qcdens of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] [coornaert-pjm] 
For $(X,d)$ Gromov-hyperbolic, let $M(\partial_g X)$ denote the collection of positive finite Borel measures on $\partial_g X $. A $G$-equivariant map $X \to M(\partial_g X)$ sending $x \to \mu_x$ is said to be a $C$ {\bf quasi-conformal density} of dimension $v$ ($v\geq 0$), for some $C\geq 1$, if
\begin{equation}
	\frac{1}{C}\exp\big(-v\beta_\xi(y,x)\big)
	\leq
	\frac{{\rm{d}}\mu_{x}}{{\rm{d}}\mu_y} (\xi)
	\leq C \exp\big(-v\beta_\xi(y,x)\big)
\end{equation}
for all $x, y \in X$, $\xi\in \partial X$. If $C=1$, it is a {\bf conformal density}. Equivalently, we also call the family of measures $(\mu_x)_{x\in G}$ a (quasi)-conformal density.
title: Defn qcdens of arXiv:2411.14350

body: In probability theory, Bernstein inequalities give bounds on the probability that the sum of random variables deviates from its mean. In the simplest case, let X_{1},..., X_{n} be independent Bernoulli random variables taking values +1 and −1 with probability 1/2 (this distribution is also known as the Rademacher distribution), then for every positive $\varepsilon$, $$\mathbb {P} \left(\left|{\frac {1}{n}}\sum _{i=1}^{n}X_{i}\right|>\varepsilon \right)\leq 2\exp \left(-{\frac {n\varepsilon ^{2}}{2(1+{\frac {\varepsilon }{3}})}}\right).$$

[Lemma 32 (Monotonicity of angles) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix a finite graph $G$, some $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Let $u$ denote some vertex, and let $E_u$ denote the set of edges incident to $u$.
    Pick
    \[
        \tau'=(\alpha',\omega',\eta')\in [0,\pi/2]^{V\setminus\{u\}}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u},
    \]
    Let $\mu_{\tau'}$ denote the measure
    $\mu_{G,\beta}$ conditioned on \[\{\tau|_{(V\setminus\{u\})\times (E\setminus E_u) \times (E\setminus E_u)}=\tau'\}.\]
    Then the density of $\alpha_u$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$
      is proportional to
    \begin{align}
        \textstyle
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\omega')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\cos\alpha_u\sum_{v \in \Gamma}\cos\alpha_v')
        \right)
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\eta')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\sin\alpha_u\sum_{v\in \Gamma}\sin\alpha_v')
        \right),
\end{align}
where $C(\rho)$ is the partition of $\{v\in V:v\sim u\}$ into $\rho$-connected components.

In particular, if $\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}$ denotes the law of $\alpha_u$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$, then
\[
    \tau'\preceq\tau''
    \qquad
    \implies
    \qquad
    \mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}\leqstoch\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau''}.
\]

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, paired). The per-output long-only stack on the relative-metric error covariance was shrunk toward the pooled simplex weights, $w_d \\mapsto w_g + (1 - s)(w_d - w_g)$. The ceiling of the family - the amount chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the calibration rows - adds $+0.59$ percent on EMIT and $+0.20$ on OCO-2 at full calibration (28 of 40 and 26 of 30 cells). A positive-part James-Stein amount $s = \\min(1, \\sum_d \\operatorname{tr} V_d / \\sum_d \\|w_d - w_g\\|^2)$ with $V_d$ the naive $n$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap covariance of the long-only weights over 20 resamples recovers $+0.10$ / $+0.15$ (worst cells $-2.6$ / $-0.0$) with amounts $0.18$ against the cross-validated $0.14$ on EMIT: it overshoots, because the long-only weights have coordinates at the boundary and the naive bootstrap is inconsistent there (Andrews 2000; resampled fits flip members between zero and positive weight). The $m$-out-of-$n$ subsampling repair ($m = n/2$, variance scaled by $m/n$; Politis-Romano) gives amounts $0.11$ / $0.12$ against $0.14$ / $0.57$ and gains $+0.43$ / $+0.09$ (worst $-1.3$ / $-0.0$). Reading: the residual pooling amount is not recoverable from resampling to the accuracy the ceiling requires and remains the one cross-validated quantity in the neighbourhood of the long-only estimator, which alone sits within that ceiling

B = 20 bootstrap resamples per fit; the CV amount from 5 folds of the calibration rows in the relative metric

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the boundary and condensation part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Use Janson's balls-in-boxes setting with weights w_j, generating function Phi, radius rho, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), nu = lim_{t up to rho} Psi(t), m/n -> lambda, pi the tilted law at tau = rho when lambda >= nu, and N_d the number of boxes with d balls. In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). In (d) the constraint is absorbed by the condensate rather than by the bulk. The record asserts that this analogue holds under regular variation of the tail, by the argument of Thevenin's Theorem 6.7 in case (d), and fails in general. The failure rests on two constructions, Theorems A and B of the companion memo on Problem 20.2. Theorem A is a subcritical law conditioned at lambda = 1 > nu, that is, sum of the xi_i equal to n-1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a non-degenerate two-point law. Theorem B is a law with nu = 1 and sigma^2 = infinity, conditioned at lambda = 1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a mixture of two Gaussians. Assuming those two theorems, a Gaussian limit for the box counts in regimes (c) and (d) does not hold without a further regularity condition on the tail. The record identifies local flatness of the tail at the scale the conditioning must supply as the dividing line. This is an unrefereed campaign result, and the counterexamples are proved in the companion memo, not in this record.
The conditioning events have positive probability.
The counterexample construction is reported, rather than proved within this record.

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.05388, 'The Efron-Stein inequality for identically distributed pairs'] For each \(i\) let \((X_i,Y_i)\) be an identically distributed pair, so that the pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\) are independent as \(i\) varies, and \(X_i\) can take at most \(k_i\) values. Let \(f\) be a bounded measurable function, and let \(Z_i=f(X_1,\ldots X_{i},Y_{i+1},\ldots Y_n)\). Then
$$
E(Z_n-Z_0)^2\le \rho(k) \sum_{i=1}^n E(Z_i-Z_{i-1})^2, \qquad \rho (k)\le \max_i k_i/2.
$$

body:
Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.
T is consistent
T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)
T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q

For a prime number $p$ and an integer $n \ge 0$, the $n$-th Morava $K$-theory at $p$ is the periodic ring spectrum $K(p, n)$ with coefficient ring $K(p, n)_* = \mathbb{F}_p[v_n, v_n^{-1}]$ with $|v_n| = 2(p^n - 1)$ for $n \ge 1$, and $K(p, 0) = H\mathbb{Q}$, $K(p, \infty) = H\mathbb{F}_p$. It is a residue field for the chromatic Balmer spectrum of finite spectra.

n \ge 0 is an integer (chromatic height)

the exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) are assumed to exist
first-passage percolation on Z^d
NO nearly-Gamma assumption on the weight law
conclusion is the single inequality chi <= 2 xi - 1, not the equality

IN THE AUTHORS' OWN WORDS: 'we show that under the assumption that exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) exist, one has the relation chi <= 2 xi - 1. One advantage of our argument is that it does not require the "nearly Gamma" assumption of Chatterjee (2013).'
WHY THE SPLIT MATTERS: quoting 'Auffinger-Damron proved the scaling relation' overstates it in two ways at once - it upgrades an inequality to an equality, and it hides that the exponents are still only assumed to exist. The other inequality's first proof appeared in a model of a Brownian particle in a Poissonian potential; in FPP a version of chi >= 2 xi - 1 goes back to Newman-Piza (1995).
SOURCE: Auffinger, A. and Damron, M. (2014), 'A simplified proof of the relation between scaling exponents in first-passage percolation', Ann. Probab. 42, no. 3, 1197-1211; arXiv:1109.0523v2.
VERIFICATION STATUS: theorem-checked-against-source. The v2 abstract states the hypothesis, the conclusion and the dropped assumption in full; the proof was not read.
title: Auffinger-Damron (2014) reprove only ONE of the two inequalities in the first-passage percolation scaling relation - they obtain chi <= 2 xi - 1, still assuming that the exponents defined in Chatterjee (2013) exist, but WITHOUT Chatterjee's 'nearly Gamma' assumption. So the nearly-Gamma hypothesis is removable for the '<=' direction and, as of the survey, not for the equality.

[Lem 7. lem: Stieltjes convergence of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Fix a metric space $(M, d^{M})$.
  Let $g_{1}, g_{2}, \ldots$ be non-decreasing functions in $D([0,1], \mathbb{R})$ 
  such that $g_{n} \to g$ in the usual $J_{1}$-Skorohod topology for some strictly increasing function $g \in D([0,1], \mathbb{R})$,
  and let $q, q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots$ be measurable functions from $[0,1]$ to $M$ such that $q_{n} \to q$ 
  in the supremum norm $\| \cdot \|_{\infty}$.
  Then, it holds that $s_{g_{n}} \circ q_{n}^{-1} \to s_{g} \circ q^{-1}$ weakly as measures on $M$.
title: Lem 7. lem: Stieltjes convergence of arXiv:2412.08236

Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Then p -> P_p(A) is a polynomial in p, hence smooth, and d/dp P_p(A) = sum_{e in E} P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p[ N(A) ], where N(A) is the number of pivotal edges. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). [Russo (1981), Margulis (1974); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.25]
A increasing and depending on finitely many coordinates
product measure with a common density p
for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands

Lewin's 2022 review discusses finite-temperature Riesz phase transitions in Section VI through nonuniqueness and symmetry breaking of Gibbs point processes, and reports numerical BCC/FCC phase diagrams in three dimensions. Its Conjecture 38 in Section IV.B instead concerns zero-temperature equilibrium configurations. Proving that conjecture, or finite phonon variance around an assumed lattice, does not by itself construct a positive-temperature crystalline Gibbs state.
Lewin review version 2, 2022-04-30
The source's finite-beta Gibbs class is stated directly for short-range s>d; long-range Gibbs specifications require separate formulation.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the recursion is integrated exactly against two published closed-form values as a control] This is the campaign answer to Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1; layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. Let e be the base of the natural logarithm. There is a constant C_star in (0,infinity) such that bar_ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_star and ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1-exp(-1/e)) C_star. More precisely, if M_star denotes the distributional limit of M_k-[k/e+(3/(2e))log k] furnished by the cited branching-random-walk minimum theorem, then C_star=E[exp(-M_star)]. In particular both tails have order exp(-k/e) k^(-3/(2e)). The proof uses Addario-Berry and Ford's Poisson-Dirichlet branching random walks, Annals of Applied Probability 23 (2013), Theorems 1.1-1.2, and Aidekon's Convergence in law of the minimum of a branching random walk, Annals of Probability 41 (2013), as stated in the record. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The stated published minimum-location, tail, and limit theorems apply to this Poisson branching walk.

$$\widetilde M_n := \mathrm{median}(M_n) = \frac ne + \frac{3}{2e}\log n + O(1), \tag{2}$$
uniformly over the class, and their Theorem 1.2 gives uniform exponential tails: for every $c_1 < e$ and $c_2 < 1$,
$$\mathbb{P}\big(M_n \le \widetilde M_n - x\big) \ll_{c_1} e^{-c_1 x}, \qquad \mathbb{P}\big(M_n \ge \widetilde M_n + x\big) \ll_{c_2} e^{-c_2 x} \qquad (n \ge 1,\ x \ge 0). \tag{3}$$

**Theorem 2.** There are absolute constants $0 < c < C < \infty$ with
$$c \le \bar\ell_k\,e^{k/e}\,k^{3/(2e)} \le C \qquad (k \ge 1),$$
that is, $\bar\ell_k = \exp[-k/e - \tfrac{3}{2e}\log k - O(1)]$. The same holds for $\ell_k$, so Conjecture 1 holds as stated.

Let X_1, X_2, ... be independent and identically distributed real random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and S_k = X_1 + ... + X_k. Define the rescaled random continuous path W_n(t) = n^{-1/2} ( S_{floor(n t)} + (n t - floor(n t)) X_{floor(n t) + 1} ) for t in [0, 1], the linear interpolation of the random walk with time scaled by n and space by sqrt(n). Then W_n converges in distribution, as a random element of C[0, 1] with the uniform norm, to a standard Brownian motion W on [0, 1]. Consequently, for every functional Phi : C[0, 1] -> R that is continuous almost surely with respect to the Wiener measure, Phi(W_n) converges in distribution to Phi(W): the law of the maximum of the walk, of its time spent positive, of its first hitting time of a level, all converge to the Brownian laws, whatever the increment distribution. The same holds in the Skorokhod space D[0, 1] for the uninterpolated step process. Finite variance is essential; with infinite variance the limits are stable processes under different scaling.

Finite-dimensional distributions: for 0 < t_1 < ... < t_k <= 1 the increments W_n(t_j) - W_n(t_{j-1}) are, up to the interpolation terms that vanish in probability, sums of about n (t_j - t_{j-1}) independent centred variables scaled by n^{-1/2}, so by the multivariate central limit theorem they converge jointly to independent normals with variances t_j - t_{j-1}: the finite-dimensional laws of Brownian motion. Tightness in C[0, 1]: W_n(0) = 0, and the modulus of continuity is controlled by a maximal inequality for the partial sums. Cut [0, 1] into about 1/delta blocks of length delta; an oscillation larger than epsilon over some pair s, t with |s - t| <= delta forces an oscillation larger than epsilon/3 inside one block, and Ottaviani's inequality bounds the probability of that by twice the tail P(|S_m| > (epsilon/3) sqrt(n) - sqrt(2 m)) with m about n delta, which by the central limit theorem is of Gaussian size, of order exp(-c epsilon^2 / delta), for large n. A union over the 1/delta blocks is then of order (1/delta) exp(-c epsilon^2 / delta), which tends to 0 as delta -> 0 uniformly in n large, and the finitely many small n are handled by the continuity of each W_n. [Lemma lem:thinning-preserves-overlap of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be finite with $|J|=n\ge2$. Choose $J_0\subseteq J$ uniformly from $\binom J{n_0}$, where $2\le n_0\le n$, and let $G_0:=G[J_0]$. Then
\[
\mathbb E\,\eta(G_0)=\eta(G).
\]
Consequently, for every $\alpha>0$,
\[
\mathbb P\big(\eta(G_0)>\alpha\big)\le\frac{\eta(G)}{\alpha}.
\]
