[Defn def.Lp-stabilizing_marking of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $\xi$ be a marking function and, depending on whether $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ is a finite or infinite marked point process, $\xi$ is defined on either finite or infinite point sets, i.e., $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times\mathbb{K}\times \hat{\mathcal{N}}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{K}'$ or $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times\mathbb{K}\times\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \longrightarrow \mathbb{K}'$.
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
We say that  $\xi$ is a {\em bounded Lipschitz-localizing marking function ({\em \textnormal{BL}-localizing} for short)} on the point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ if 
there 
is an increasing-decreasing family of 
functions~$\varphi_p: [0, \infty) \to [0,1], p \in \mathbb{N},$ such that 
\begin{align} 
 \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in \mathbb{R}^d} 
 d_{\textnormal{BL}, \bk x1p}( \bk\xi1p(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}),\bk{\xi^{(r)}}1p( \tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))  \leq 2\varphi_p(r), \ r  \geq 0, 
\end{align}
where the extra notation $\bk x1p$ in $d_{\textnormal{BL}, \bk x1p}$ accounts for the distribution of the vector of scores  $\bk {\xi}1p(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})$ and $ \bk{\xi^{(r)}}1p( \tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))$ under the Palm distribution $\mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p}$ of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$. 

\item  We say that   $\xi$  is {\em  \textnormal{BL}-localizing  on the finite  windows}
  of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ if there is an increasing-decreasing family of functions  $\varphi_p: [0, \infty) \to [0,1], p \in \mathbb{N}$,
  such that
\begin{align} 
  \sup_{1 \leq n < \infty} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in W_n} d_{\textnormal{BL}, \bk x1p}\big( \bk{\xi}1p(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n),\bk{\xi^{(r)}}1p( \tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n)) \big)  \leq 2\varphi_p(r), \ r  \geq 0.
\end{align}

\item  We say that $\xi$ is {\em fast \textnormal{BL}-localizing} on $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, or on the finite windows of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$, if $(\varphi_p)_{p \in \mathbb{N}}$ are  fast decreasing. 

\item  Exponential \textnormal{BL}-localization signifies that  $\varphi_p$ is exponentially decreasing to zero  for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$.   
\end{enumerate}

 As elsewhere, in~(equation Lp-stab-infinite of the paper) and~(equation Lp-stab of the paper) we adopt the
convention that the supremum over $\bk{x}{1}{p}$ is understood as an
$\mathrm{ess\,sup}$ with respect to the factorial moment measures of the
common ground process~$\mathcal{P}$, which are tacitly assumed to have  the form $\rho^{(p)}(\bk x1p)\mathrm{d} \bk{x}{1}{p}$ with $\rho^{(p)}$ uniformly bounded by $\kappa_p$.
title: \BL-localization of marking functions

body: In the mathematical discipline of group theory, Cayley's theorem, named in honour of Arthur Cayley, states that every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group. More specifically, G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group whose elements are the permutations of the underlying set of G. Explicitly,for each , the left-multiplication-by-g map sending each element x to gx is a permutation of G, and the map sending each element g to is an injective homomorphism, so it defines an isomorphism from G onto a subgroup of .

[Dfn 118 (occupation measures, continuous-time) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\vY^\frozen$ be the subsequential limit from Theorem~\ref{t:tightness}. Similarly to Definitions~\ref{ss:sde.abstract}
and \ref{d:discrete.occ},
let $\rho_{\vY}$ be the occupation measure for $\vY^\frozen=(\vY^{\frozen,\RomI:\RomIII},Y^{\frozen,\Ising})$. We also let
$\rho_D$, $\rho_V$, $\rho_U$, $\rho_\rrr$, $\rho_\www$
be the occupation measures for
$D^{\frozen,\RomI}$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomII}$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomII,\RomIII}$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomIII}$, and $Q^{\frozen,\Ising}$ respectively: for instance, $\rho_D$ is the signed measure such that
	\[\int_{\R^5}
	f(t,\vy)\rho_D(dt\,d\vy)
	= \bE\int_0^1
	f(t,\vY^\frozen,(t))
	\,dD^\frozen(t)\]
for any bounded continuous function $f$ on $\R^5$. Note it 
follows from Theorem~\ref{t:tightness} that $D^\frozen$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomII}$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomII,\RomIII}$, $Q^{\frozen,\RomIII}$, and $Q^{\frozen,\Ising}$ are finite-variation processes, so the integrals with respect to these processes are well-defined. Denote the conditional measures $\rho_t\equiv \rho_{\vY,t}$, $\rho_{D,t}$, etc. Note that since $(Y^{\frozen,\RomI},Y^{\frozen,\RomII},Y^{\frozen,\RomIII})$ evolves independently of $Y^{\frozen,\Ising}$,
we can factorize
 $\rho_t=\varrho_t\otimes\varsigma_t$,
 $\rho_{D,t}=\varrho_{D,t}\otimes\varsigma_t$, and so on.
title: occupation measures, continuous-time

[Theorem thm:pole-calibration of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Let $x_0=0$, let $b_a$ be defined by (equation eq:pole-reference-drift of the paper), and suppose
(equation eq:pole-coefficient-class of the paper) holds.  There exists
$K_{\mathrm{th}}=K_{\mathrm{th}}(T,\lambda,\Lambda)\geq1$ such that the following
holds.  For each $0<\theta<1$, define the threshold
\begin{equation}
 K_\theta^\star(a):=K_{\mathrm{th}}\theta^{-1}\mathcal M_d(a).
 
\end{equation}
Choose any $K\geq K_\theta^\star(a)$.  Set
$\omega_K(t):=e^{-K(T-t)/2}$ and, for
$\alpha\geq0$, write
$\overline w_{\alpha,K}(t):=t^\alpha\omega_K(t)$.  For
$\kappa\geq0$, set
$w_{\alpha,K;\kappa}:=(\overline w_{\alpha,K})_\kappa$ according to
Definition~(def:regular-time-weight of the paper).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The reference pair $(b_a,a)$ satisfies
Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) and~(ass:bochner-regularity of the paper).
Its time-$t$ diffusion law is $\mu_t=\gamma_t=N(0,tI_d)$, with current
velocity $c(t,y)=y/(2t)$.
\item If $\alpha\geq1/2$, then
\begin{equation}
 C_{\overline w_{\alpha,K}}(X^a)\leq2/\sqrt{1-\theta}.
 
\end{equation}
\item If $0\leq\alpha<1/2$ and
$0<\theta<1-4/(C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}})^2$,
put
\begin{equation*}
 \Delta_{\mathrm{hi}}
 :=1-\theta-\frac4{(C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}})^2}>0.
\end{equation*}
There are constants with the following dependencies:
\begin{equation*}
 C=C\bigl(T,\lambda,\Lambda,\alpha,\theta,\Delta_{\mathrm{hi}}^{-1}\bigr)>0,
 \qquad
 \kappa_0=\kappa_0\bigl(
   T,\lambda,\Lambda,\alpha,\theta,\Delta_{\mathrm{hi}}^{-1},\mathcal M_d(a)
 \bigr)\geq1
\end{equation*}
For every $\kappa\geq\kappa_0$, these constants give
\begin{equation}
 C_{w_{\alpha,K;\kappa}}(X^a)
 \leq C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}}
 +C\mathcal M_d(a)
  \left(\frac{\log(2+\kappa)}{\kappa}\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
The same $C$ and $\kappa_0$ apply to every $K\geq K_\theta^\star(a)$ in
(equation eq:pole-weight-threshold of the paper).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:pole-calibration of arXiv:2608.16119

[Definition 14 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] We define the following two bornologies:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For a family of bornological spaces $\{(S_\lambda, \mathcal{B}_\lambda)\}_{\lambda\in \Lambda}$, the set-theoretical direct product $\Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda}\mathcal{B}_\lambda$ forms a bornological base on $\Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda} S_\lambda$.
        We call $\langle \Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda}\mathcal{B}_\lambda\rangle$ the \emph{direct product bornology} on $\Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda} S_\lambda$.
        \item Let $P$ be a set and $f$ a map from $P$ to the bornological space $S$.
        Then the family $f^*\mathcal{B}_S:=\{f^{-1}(B)\subset P\mid B\in \mathcal{B}_S\}$ forms a bornological base on $P$.
        We call $\langle f^*\mathcal{B}_S \rangle $ the \emph{inverse image bornology} of $\mathcal{B}_S$ by the map $f$. 
        In particular, if $P$ is a subset of $S$ and the map $f$ is the inclusion map, the bornology $f^*\mathcal{B}_S =\langle f^*\mathcal{B}_S \rangle $ is called the \emph{subbornology} of $\mathcal{B}_S$.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Definition 14 of arXiv:2608.25785

[Lemma lem-lf-resample-4 of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3, \beta_4 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in (1, \infty)$.
	     Suppose $\psi\sim \mathrm{LF}_\mathbb{H}^{(\beta_1, 0), (\beta_2, 1), (\beta_3, x), (\beta_4, \infty)}$. Let $\mathfrak h$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb{H}$ whose values on $(0,x)$ agree with those of $\psi$ and which has normal derivative zero on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (x, \infty)$. Conditioned on $\mathfrak h$, we have $\psi \stackrel d= h + \mathfrak h + (\frac{\beta_2}2 -Q) G(\cdot, \infty)$ where $h$ is a GFF on $\mathbb{H}$ with zero boundary conditions on $(0,x)$ and free boundary conditions on $(-\infty, 0) \cup (x, \infty)$, and $G$ is the Green function of $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem-lf-resample-4 of arXiv:2411.19810

body:
For every measure space (X, Sigma, mu) and every 1 <= p <= infinity, L^p(mu) is complete, hence a Banach space. Moreover, for p < infinity, if f_n -> f in L^p then some subsequence converges to f mu-a.e., and there is a dominating function: a subsequence f_{n_k} and h in L^p with |f_{n_k}| <= h a.e. for all k. For p = infinity, L^infinity-convergence is uniform convergence outside a single null set. Equivalent series form: if sum_n ||f_n||_p < infinity then sum_n f_n converges absolutely a.e. and in L^p. (For 0 < p < 1 the space is complete for the metric d(f,g) = ||f-g||_p^p.)
(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space
1 <= p <= infinity
functions identified mu-a.e.

body:
Own-work draft; proof (unaudited). Let d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2,1<=r<K be integers. There are d pairs of contexts, one arbitrary A and one systematic S per pair, and N-2d known S contexts. S has all K candidates true; each A has an independent uniform r-subset. The target p chooses contexts uniformly and then truths uniformly. The orientation class has VC dimension d. Observe n iid factual context/candidate samples WITHOUT partition tags. Independently conditional on the world, a perfect verifier supplies a uniform r-subset T_x of truths in EVERY variable context, including S, without orientation labels. This reveals every A truth. Set kappa=1-r/K. A pair is resolved exactly if a training sample lies outside either T_x. If U pairs remain unresolved, exactly 2^U worlds are compatible, though their actual posterior probabilities need not be equal. For arbitrary generator g, source Mis_infinity is TV(g,p_Pi), with p uniformly coarsened within exact g-probability level sets. Require Mis_infinity<=c in EVERY compatible world. The exact conditional worst-world false-mass frontier is V(c,U)=(kappa*U/N-c)_+/2 for 0<=c<=1. A uniform COMPATIBLE-WORLD average is an artificial lower-bound device, not an assertion about the actual posterior. An invariant-group generator attains V in every world. At c=0 every robustly feasible g has false mass at least kappa*U/(2N) in EACH actual compatible world, by a separate finite-cell inequality. Therefore the exact GLOBAL minimax expected false mass at zero budget is kappa*d/(2N)*(1-kappa/N)^n. The joint occupancy PGF is sum_{j=0}^d binom(d,j)*(z-1)^j*(1-j*kappa/N)^n, without independence of missing-pair indicators. For c>0 only E[(kappa*U/(2N)-c)_+] <= global value <= E[(kappa*U/N-c)_+]/2 is claimed. Expected conditional worst-world value need not equal global minimax expectation. The zero-budget value is kappa/2 times the error of the specified fair completion of support-consistent ERM, not a claim about optimal statistical classification error. This is full verification with extra S certificates, robust calibration, and an explicit paired VC family; it is not the general partial-verifier or actual-world-only calibration problem. Independent audit and priority review pending.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ce641672c77772014d04c0f0fc8229c909dd1c1453222974535345804389f4b3","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ce/ce641672c77772014d04c0f0fc8229c909dd1c1453222974535345804389f4b3.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:53d58ec2cda38bfc21fe0da89da7bb92798ef336c1b995aec1105ac63f2c6488","bundle_entry_key":"untagged-full-verifier-frontier","bundle_id":"population.t379-untagged-full-verifier-frontier-20261020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; verified truth supports","draft":"w709/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.calibration:untagged-full-support-verifier-frontier","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Full truth supports without orientation labels: untagged all-sample frontier

Candidate T379-C013 v2, proof (unaudited). Exact rational checks PASS;
independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending.
Target 2, with target-1 interaction. This treats ell=r, not arbitrary
partial verification. The hardest open extension is the unresolved
untagged posterior with ell<r and arbitrary positive calibration budgets.

## Experiment and compatible worlds

Integers d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2 and 1<=r<K. There are d pairs with
exactly one A and one S context; other contexts are known S. Each S has
all K truths; each A has an independent uniform r-subset of truths. The
factual law is uniform on contexts then uniformly true within context.
Observe n iid factual samples with NO A/S tags. Independently after
training a perfect verifier supplies an r-subset T_x of true candidates
in EVERY variable context, uniformly among r-subsets of truths, without
orientation tags. Thus it reveals ALL truths in A, and r truths in S.
The verified fraction of arbitrary truths is one; the additional S
truths are explicitly part of this information protocol.

A context containing an observed candidate outside T_x must be S.
An A context can never do so. If neither sibling in a pair has such an
observation, both orientations are compatible, even if observations
inside T_x make their LIKELIHOODS unequal. Let U count these unresolved
pairs. Resolved pairs have known S and A supports; in an unresolved
pair the A support would be exactly T_x under either orientation.
Consequently the compatible world set has exactly 2^U orientations,
and no other unknown support variables.

Put kappa=1-r/K, lambda=1/(NK) and p0=kappa/N. The proposed exact
conditional WORST-WORLD robust Mis_infinity frontier over all g is

 V(c,U)=(kappa*U/N-c)_+/2,         0<=c<=1.                (1)

Here feasibility requires source miscalibration <=c for EVERY compatible
world; output bins are the exact g-probability levels. The actual
posterior-average game is not asserted to have this value: its
orientation weights can be unequal after untagged factual observations.

At ZERO calibration budget a stronger pointwise conclusion holds:

 H_theta(g)>=kappa*U/(2N) for EVERY compatible theta,       (2)

for every robustly zero-calibrated g. An attainer has equality in every
world. Therefore the GLOBAL minimax expected value at zero budget is

 inf_A sup_world E[H(A(data,T))]
       =kappa*d/(2N)*(1-kappa/N)^n.                       (3)

This global value does not follow just by averaging a conditional
worst-world lower bound; the separate pointwise argument below is needed.

## Conditional frontier with an artificial uniform compatible prior

For a conditional worst-world lower bound, average the compatible
orientations UNIFORMLY. This is an admissible proof device even though
it is generally NOT the Bayesian posterior given the actual samples.
Let mu be the mean factual law under this artificial distribution. There
are three atom types:

 F: known false atoms of resolved A contexts, mu=0;
 M: atoms outside T_x in unresolved pairs, mu=lambda/2;
 S: all atoms safe in every compatible world, mu>=lambda.

In M the uniform-compatible-prior false risk is 1/2; in F it is one;
in S it is zero. The mu mass of M is kappa*U/N. In any uniform
coarsening Pi, mu_Pi(F union M)>=mu(F union M), since inside densities
are <=lambda/2 and outside safe densities are >=lambda. Linearity and
TV convexity show TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c for every robustly feasible g, using
its fixed bins Pi(g). Hence

 max_theta H_theta(g)>=average_theta H_theta(g)
    =g(F)+g(M)/2 >= (kappa*U/N-c)_+/2.

For attainment, begin from mu, remove min(c,kappa*U/N) uniformly from
M and add it uniformly to the fixed S reservoir. Keep F at zero.
Within each unresolved pair, both siblings' certified atoms have equal
g, and both siblings' outside atoms have equal g; their pairwise p
masses are invariant across orientations. Known safe/false groups have
invariant p masses too. Every exact score bin is a union of these
groups, so p_Pi=mu_Pi for every theta, including merged or zero scores.
Since g_Pi=g, Mis_infinity<=TV(mu,g)<=c. Every actual world has half
of M's candidate atoms false, giving H_theta=V(c,U) worldwise.
This proves (1), without substituting actual posterior weights.

## Pointwise zero-budget lower bound

Suppose g is robustly calibrated with budget zero, and fix ANY actual
compatible world theta. Then g=p_theta,Pi for all theta, with Pi the
exact score partition. Averaging worlds uniformly gives g=mu_Pi.

In a cell B, let c_B count M-atoms false in this actual theta, d_B
count M-atoms true there, f_B count globally false F-atoms, and t_B
count universally safe S-atoms. Put L=c_B+d_B+f_B+t_B>0. We have

 mu(B)>=lambda*((c_B+d_B)/2+t_B).

The false mass assigned by mu_Pi in this cell is therefore at least

 lambda*(c_B+d_B+2*t_B)*(c_B+f_B)/(2*L)
                  >=lambda*c_B/2,

because the numerator difference after multiplying by 2L/lambda is

 d_B*f_B+c_B*t_B+2*t_B*f_B >=0.

Sum cells. Exactly U*(K-r) M-atoms are false in each world. Thus
H_theta(g)>=lambda*U*(K-r)/2=kappa*U/(2N), proving (2).
This is an analytic finite-cell inequality, not a sample-based claim.
It allows arbitrary cells and known-false dilution atoms.

For positive c, TV(mu_Pi,g)<=c instead gives the useful pointwise
bound H_theta(g)>=(kappa*U/(2N)-c)_+. It does NOT give the stronger
conditional-worst-world expression (1) for each theta. We do not infer
an exact global positive-budget minimax value from (1).

## Actual sampling and exact expectation at zero budget

Fix an actual world and verifier output T. Its training samples remain
iid, since T was independently drawn conditional on the world. Pair j
is resolved exactly when a sample hits its S context outside T_x, an
event of mass (K-r)/(NK)=p0 per draw. These distinguishing categories
are disjoint across pairs. Thus, without any independence assumption on
missing-category indicators,

 E[U]=d*(1-p0)^n,
 E[z^U]=sum_{j=0}^d binom(d,j)*(z-1)^j*(1-j*p0)^n.        (4)

The joint missing event for j specified categories has probability
(1-j*p0)^n; expand the product of missing-indicator factors to obtain
the PGF. This law is independent of the actual supports, orientations
and identity of T. Pointwise (2) supplies the expected lower bound in
EVERY fixed world; the preceding generator attains equality in every
outcome at c=0. This proves (3) for the global minimax game.

For c>0 the global expected minimax is bracketed by

 E[(kappa*U/(2N)-c)_+] <= value
                  <= (1/2)*E[(kappa*U/N-c)_+].           (5)

These agree at c=0, but are not generally the same elsewhere.
The expectation of the conditional worst-world value IS the upper
expression; it is a different objective from global minimax expectation.

A specified fair completion of unresolved support-consistent ERM bits
has expected classification error d/N*(1-p0)^n, so (3) is kappa/2
times that specified ERM error. This is NOT claimed to be the minimax
statistical classification error: likelihoods of inside-T observations
can help classify unresolved pairs. Robust calibration retains all
compatible worlds regardless of their likelihood.

Union bound P(U>0)<=d*(1-p0)^n gives a probability >=1-delta regime
of completely known partition when n>=(N/kappa)*log(d/delta). The
algorithm uses certificate flags and group sampling in polynomial time,
with O(n+d*r) explicitly supplied truth identities. No NK table is needed.

## Scope and primary-source basis

The source coarsening definition is Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3,
Definitions 1--2,pp.8--9. This experiment has a strong full-support
verifier that also reveals r truths in every S context; revealing only
A truth sets WITH their types is a different and easier protocol.
The result assumes robust calibration over all compatible worlds, not
merely calibration in the actual world with high probability. No novelty
is claimed for coupon occupancy or the elementary TV inequalities.
The proposed result is the exact explicit untagged verifier frontier and
its pointwise lower bound at zero error. The exact check log is
logs/untagged_full_verifier_check.txt: 6560 integer-cell inequalities,
all 203 six-atom partitions, 9842 ten-atom partitions with at most three
cells, 16 attainer/world checks and 21 joint occupancy laws pass.
Negative controls cover safe-density removal and a genuinely skewed
posterior whose mean law fails robust calibration. These finite checks
support, and do not replace, the general derivation above. Independent
audit and primary-source priority review remain required.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:7386f14ca4bfc1ec9d2c93ba2c3b11ca80db85498ac05adfffcfdf31e3c50eda","revision_digest":"sha256:f09de852daeee9aa748fa6bd13e798b52467eedb9678379dfbfb49901061d3bc","source_id":"owner:w709:T379-C013:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20T12:04:52.354544+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Splitting the mean over the depth-r boundary layer and its complement gives |E S_V/|V|-rho_infinity|<=epsilon_r+|boundary_layer_r(V)|/|V|. For each fixed r, the last ratio vanishes along lattice Folner exhaustions; then r can grow after V. Check: Occupation indicators lie between zero and one, so the entire boundary contribution is bounded by its cardinality. A fixed-depth boundary layer has size at most a constant depending on d,r times |boundary V|. Obstruction: Ordinary local convergence at a fixed origin does not give the required uniform interior estimate. A growing central defect can have zero volume fraction but determine every fixed-window limit.

[Proposition prop:tailbnd of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let \(\Phi\) be a coupling of \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) which is antipodally symmetric, i.e., \(\Phi\) is invariant under the antipodal map \(T: (v_1,v_2) \mapsto (-v_1,-v_2)\) for all \((v_1,v_2) \in (S^{d-1})^2\).
    Given the coupling $(Z_0^{(1)},Z_0^{(2)})$ defined by (equation eq:couplingZeroCells of the paper) using \(\Phi\), we have for all $u \in S^{d-1}$ and $t > 0$,
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}[ \rho_{Z_0^{(1)}}(u)- \rho_{Z_0^{(2)}}(u) \geq t]
        &= 2 \gamma \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-\gamma F_u(y+t,y)} \int_{(S^{d-1})^2} \langle u,v_2 \rangle   \indic{ 0 < \langle  u , v_2\rangle < \frac{y+t}{t} \langle u,v_2-v_1 \rangle} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \Phi (v_1 , v_2) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} y,
    \end{align*}
    where $F_u(\cdot,\cdot)$ is defined as in (equation def:Fu of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:tailbnd of arXiv:2608.13452

[Theorem thm:positive-random-measure-realization of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(X,\mu,Y)$ be a separated cross-section system. For every
$R>0$, there is an equivariant Borel map
$\Phi_R:X\to\mathcal M_+(\mathbb R^d)$ such that
\[
    \Phi_R(x)=g_x\,\lambda_d,
    \qquad
    0<
    \inf_{\substack{x\in X\\u\in\mathbb R^d}}
    g_x(u),
    \qquad
    \sup_{\substack{x\in X\\u\in\mathbb R^d}}
    |\partial^\alpha g_x(u)|
    <\infty
    \quad
    (\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d).
\]
The pushforward
$\zeta_R:=(\Phi_R)_*\mu$ has local second moments and satisfies
\[
    \sigma_{\zeta_R}\bigl(B_R(0)\bigr)=0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    \Phi_R(x)=\Phi_R(x')
    \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    \kappa_Y(x)=\kappa_Y(x').
\]
Consequently, if $Y$ is generating, then $\Phi_R$ is a measurable
$\mathbb R^d$-isomorphism from $(X,\mu)$ to
$\bigl(\mathcal M_+(\mathbb R^d),\zeta_R\bigr)$. The measure
$\zeta_R$ is ergodic whenever $\mu$ is ergodic.

[Prop CLEcoupling1 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Consider a zero boundary GFF $\Phi_D$ on $D$ and the nested CLE$_4$ determined by exploring consecutively two-valued sets $A_{-2\lambda, 2\lambda}$. Then, for all boundary conditions $v \in 2\lambda \mathbb{Z}$, we have the following properties in coupling with $\Phi_D + v$: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The labels $s_\ell \in \{-2\lambda, 2\lambda\}$ attached to each loop $\ell \in \text{CLE}_4^{n}$ are i.i.d. symmetric conditionally on the loops, 
and in terms of distributions,
$$\sum_{\Gamma \in \text{CLE}^{\rm nest}_4}(v1_{\Gamma \text{ outermost}}+s_\Gamma)
\1_{\operatorname{Int}(\Gamma)} = \Phi_D +v.$$
\item 
We assign the height $v$ to the boundary of the domain. Thereby, each gasket in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ can be uniquely attached a height corresponding to the sum of labels of loops $s_\ell$ in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ strictly surrounding this gasket, including the boundary of the domain. If this sum equals $h$, then we say that the gasket is at height $h$. Equivalently we can attach a height to each loop in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ by considering the sum of labels of loops surrounding and including this loop and the boundary. This way the height of the gasket corresponds to the height of its outermost loop.   
\item In this coupling, conditionally on the loops, for each $z \in D$, the heights $h$ of the gaskets in 
CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ surrounding $z$ form a simple symmetric random walk $S^z(m)$ with step-size $2\lambda$ and starting point $v$. 
\item For $v \neq 0$, consider $A_0$, the first passage set of $\Phi_D + v$ with boundary values $0$. Then $A_0$ is almost surely equal to taking the connected component of the boundary of the closed union of all gaskets of non-zero height. In particular, for each $z \in D \cap \mathbb{Q}^2$, the boundary of the connected component of 
$D \setminus A_0$ containing $z$ is constructed as follows: we consider the nested loop sequence surrounding $z$ until the first time that a loop of height $0$ appears and that is the boundary. 
\item Further, the sign excursion sets of $\Phi_D + v$ have the following description using nested CLE$_4$: we consider the closed union of all the gaskets in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ of height different than zero. The connected components have then the law of sign excursion sets.
\item Finally, the dual of the excursion sets, i.e. the complement of the excursion sets in $D$, is given by the disjoint union of all the gaskets of height $0$ in the nested CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$. 
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 5 (Chebotarev density theorem) of arXiv:2609.02444, 'The Hasse norm principle for $A_4$-quartic extensions of global function fields'] Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\phi \colon X \to Y\) a \(G\)-torsor defined over \(\FF_q\), and \(\Phi \subset G\) a conjugacy class.
  \begin{enumerate}
      \item  Suppose that \(X\) is geometrically connected.
  Then
  \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\{y \in Y(\FF_{q^m}) \mid \varphi(y) = \Phi\}|}{|Y(\FF_{q^m})|} = \frac{|\Phi|}{|G|}. \]
  \item More generally, suppose that \(Y\) is geometrically connected and \(X\) has \(r\) geometric components, all defined over \(\FF_q\).
  Then
  \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\{y \in Y(\FF_{q^{m}}) \mid \varphi(y) = \Phi\}|}{|Y(\FF_{q^{m}})|} \leq r\frac{|\Phi|}{|G|}, \]
  with equality if and only if $\Phi$ is contained in the stabiliser of a geometric component of $X$.
  \end{enumerate}

[Theorem kernel of arXiv:2606.19507, 'The $t$-Split Two-Periodic Aztec Diamond Model'] Let $-N \leq \xi,\xi' \leq -1$ and $0 < m, m' < N$. The correlation kernel $t$-split two-periodic Aztec diamond of size $2N$ with $t < 1/2$ can be written as a piecewise expression depending on whether $m' \leq tN$ or $m' > tN$. For $0 < m' \leq tN$ the kernel is:
    \begin{multline} 
        \left[\mathbb{K}_N(4m',2\xi'+j;4m,2\xi+i)\right]_{i,j=0,1} = -\frac{\1_{m>m'}}{2\pi \mathrm{i}} \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z} z^{\xi'-\xi}\phi_{m'\to m,N}(z)\\
        +\frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1} \mathrm{d}w \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\alpha,1}(w)^{tN-m'}F_{\alpha,1}(w) \\
        \times \Phi_{\beta}(w)^{(1/2-t)N} \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1}\mathrm{d}w\oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\alpha,2}(w)^{tN-m'} c(w) F_{\alpha,2}(w) F_{\beta,1}(w)F_{\alpha,1}(w) \\
        \Phi_{\beta}(w)^{(1/2-t)N} \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N} \Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z).
    \end{multline}
    For $tN < m' < N$ the kernel is:
    \begin{multline} 
        \left[\mathbb{K}_N(4m',2\xi'+j;4m,2\xi+i)\right]_{i,j=0,1} = - \frac{\1_{m>m'}}{2\pi\mathrm{i}} \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z} z^{\xi'-\xi} \phi_{m' \to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1} \mathrm{d}w \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\beta,1}(w)^{N/2-m'} F_{\beta,1}(w)\\
        \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1}\mathrm{d}w\oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\beta,1}(w)^{(2t - 1/2)N - m'}c(w)F_{\beta,1}(w)F_{\alpha,1}(w)F_{\beta,2}(w)\\
        \times \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z). 
    \end{multline}
    In both cases, $\gamma_1$ is a simple, positively oriented contour surrounding $1$ but not $0$, while $\gamma_{0,1}$ is a simple, positively oriented contour surrounding both $0$ and $1$ with $\gamma_1$ in its interior. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let f be a continuous complex-valued function on an open connected subset U of C. If for every closed triangular path T whose closed solid triangle lies inside U, the contour integral of f around the boundary of T equals zero, then f is holomorphic on U. Morera's theorem is essentially the converse of the Cauchy-Goursat theorem, and it is commonly used to prove that a function built as a locally uniform limit, series, or integral of holomorphic functions is itself holomorphic.
title: Morera's theorem

Let U be an open subset of R^D and L be C^3 on a neighborhood of the gradient-flow trajectories in question. For every x in U suppose the solution phi_t(x) of d phi_t/dt=-grad L(phi_t), phi_0=x, exists for all t>=0 and converges to Phi(x). Assume the resulting endpoint map Phi:U->R^D is C^2. Then for every x in U, D Phi(x) grad L(x)=0 and D^2 Phi(x)[grad L(x),grad L(x)]=-D Phi(x) Hess L(x) grad L(x). Here the second derivative of the vector-valued map is a bilinear map. The identities hold on the domain of the endpoint map, not merely at its limiting minima. They assert annihilation of grad L; they do not assert annihilation of every individual noise direction in a multi-output loss. Source: Li, Wang and Arora, What Happens after SGD Reaches Zero Loss? -- A Mathematical Framework, Lemma C.2, PDF p29.

Independently checked proof (PASS w667 and w668): C002 v1. For d>=2, every rotation-invariant Borel law F on R^d is n-CM for every n>=2 with constant sum zero, without moment assumptions. Let R have the radius law of F and let Q be an independent Haar-distributed orthogonal matrix. For fixed unit vectors v_j forming a planar regular n-gon, set X_j=RQv_j. Haar invariance gives each full marginal F and sum_j v_j=0 gives sum_j X_j=0. Affine images remain n-CM; uniform ellipsoids follow from affine images of uniform balls. Uniform intervals follow separately by projecting uniform S^2, whose coordinate law is uniform on [-1,1]. An arbitrary symmetric law on R is not asserted to be odd-order CM. No novelty claim.
d>=2 for general rotation-invariant law
n>=2 integer
Common radius and Haar rotation independent of each other
Uniform interval handled by projection from dimension three

[Lem 64 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have
$\sM^{\si}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sii}(\alpha,q_0)$.

\begin{proof} We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\FAIRdefn\\
	\TMPONEdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
We see that the $\si$ and $\sii$ classes differ only in the condition on the Ising initialization $Y(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$: the $\si$ class satisfies the condition~\ref{it:7.1} (i.e., $\zeta^{\Ising} \in \cP_2(\R)$), while the $\sii$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:7.2} (i.e., $\zeta^{\Ising} \in \cP([-1,1])$).

Therefore, let us suppose we have controls $(q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the $(\alpha,q_0,L,\epsilon)$-$\si$ conditions, which drive processes $X,Y$ as in \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}, \eqref{e:formal.sde.ising}. We will construct controls $(\tilde q_*,\tilde b,\tilde \sigma,\tilde w,\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the $(\alpha,q_0,L,\tilde{\epsilon})$-$\sii$ conditions, for some $\tilde{\epsilon}$ that will tend to zero as $\epsilon\to0$. The latter controls will drive processes $\tilde X, \tilde Y$ that will approximate $X,Y$.

Let $(\tilde q_*,\tilde b,\tilde \sigma,\tilde p,\tilde \zeta) = (q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$.
    We then take 
    \[\tilde\zeta^{\Ising}
    =f_\# \zeta^{\Ising},\quad
        f(x) = \begin{cases}
            1 - \epsilon/x
            & 
            \textup{for $x \in (1,+\infty)$,} \\
            (1-\epsilon) x &
            \textup{for $[-1,1]$,} \\
            -1 + \epsilon/x &
            \textup{for $x \in (-\infty,1)$.}
        \end{cases}
    \]
Thus $\tilde\zeta^{\Ising} \in \cP([-1,1])$, so it satisfies condition~\ref{it:7.2}. We couple the initializations $Y(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$ and 
	\[
	\tilde{Y}(q_*)
	=f(Y(q_*))
	\sim \tilde{\zeta}^\Ising\,.
	\]
Note that for $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, the function $f$ is an invertible mapping from $\bbR$ to $(-1,1)$.
    Recall from the definition \eqref{e:filt.X.Y} of $\cF_Y$ that we can write
    \[
        w_t = w_t\Big((W(s))_{s\in [q_*,t]},U',Y(q_*)\Big)\,,
    \]
where the $w_t$ on the right-hand side is a measurable function. We then define $\tilde w$ by setting
    \[
        \tilde w_t\Big((W(s))_{s\in [q_*,t]},U',\tilde Y(q_*)\Big)
        = w_t\Big(
        (W(s))_{s\in [q_*,t]},
        U',
        f^{-1}(\tilde Y(q_*))
        = Y(q_*) 
        \Big)\,.
    \]
Therefore $w=\tilde{w}$ as processes.
We let $\tilde X, \tilde Y$ be defined by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} and \eqref{e:formal.sde.ising} with $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma,\tilde w)$ in place of $(b,\sigma,w)$; and we couple them to
$X,Y$ by taking the initializations $\tilde X(q_*) = X(q_*)$ and $\tilde Y(q_*) = f(Y(q_*))$, as well as the same 
Brownian motions $B,W$. It is clear from these definitions that conditions \ref{it:1.2}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.2}, \ref{it:4.1}, \ref{it:8.1} remain satisfied for $(\tilde q_*,\tilde b,\tilde \sigma,\tilde w,\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising)$; so it remains to verify that conditions \ref{it:5.1} and \ref{it:6.1} remain satisfied.

From the above definitions and \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}, it is clear that $X=\tilde{X}$ as processes. Since we already noted that $w=\tilde{w}$ as processes, it follows from \eqref{e:formal.sde.ising} that
	\beq
	Y(t)-Y(q_*)
	= \int_{q_*}^t w_u\,d W(u)
	=\tilde{Y}(t)-\tilde{Y}(q_*)
	\eeq
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. Thus, conditions
\ref{it:5.1} and \ref{it:6.1} will essentially follow from showing that
$Y(q_*)$ and $\tilde{Y}(q_*)$ are close in $L^2$, so we turn to this next.

Let $g(x) = (|x|-1)_+^2$. Recall from Remark~\ref{r:true.mg} that $Y$ is an $L^2$-bounded continuous martingale. Since $g$ is nonnegative and convex, it follows that $g(Y(t))$ is a nonnegative submartingale. Thus
    \[
    \E g(Y(q_*))
    \le \E g(Y(1)) 
    \le \E\Big[(|Y(1)|-1)^2\Big]
    \le \epsilon\,,
    \]
where the last inequality follows from condition~\ref{it:5.1} for $Y(1) (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary projected-unit-sphere of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] Let
		\(
		\bar g=\bar g(\omega_3)
		\in C^{0,\beta}(S)
		\)
		be axially symmetric. Define
		\begin{equation}
			{\rm c}[\bar g]
			=
			-
			\frac{
				\displaystyle
				\int_S\bar g\,\omega_3\,d\sigma
			}{
				\displaystyle
				\int_S\omega_3^2\,d\sigma
			}.
		\end{equation}
		Then there exists a unique axially symmetric
		\(
		\bar h\in C^{2,\beta}(S)
		\)
		satisfying
		$$
		J_S[\bar h]
		=
		\bar g
		+
		{\rm c}[\bar g]\,\omega_3,
		\qquad
		\bar h(P_S)=0.
		$$
		Moreover,
		\begin{equation}
			\|\bar h\|_{C^{2,\beta}(S)}
			+
			|{\rm c}[\bar g]|
			\le
			C
			\|\bar g\|_{C^{0,\beta}(S)}.
		\end{equation}
		We denote this linear solution operator by
		\begin{equation}
			\mathcal T_S[\bar g]
			=
			(\bar h,{\rm c}[\bar g]).
		\end{equation}

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that
\(\int_\Omega m(x)\varphi_{1,\Omega}^{\alpha+1}\,dx<0\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[a)]
If $|\Omega^+|>0$, then there exists a non-negative weak solution
$u_{\lambda^*}^+$ of \eqref{Eq1} such that
\[
E_{\lambda^*}(u_{\lambda^*}^+)<0,
\qquad
E_{\lambda^*}''(u_{\lambda^*}^+)>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)
\rightarrow E_{\lambda^*}(u_{\lambda^*}^+)
\qquad\text{as }\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*.
\]

\item[b)]
If $|\Omega^0\cup\Omega^+|>0$ and condition \textbf{(M)} holds, then
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)\rightarrow0
\qquad\text{as }\lambda\uparrow\lambda^*.
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family {A_i : i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by any set I, there exists a choice function c defined on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently: every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting one element from each. Over the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms ZF, the axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma and to the well-ordering theorem, and also to Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC is independent of ZF: Godel (1938) showed ZF plus AC is consistent if ZF is (constructible universe), and Cohen (1963) showed ZF plus the negation of AC is consistent if ZF is (forcing). Countable and finite choices do not follow from ZF alone in general, but AC is provable in ZF for finite index sets I by induction.

[Theorem Thm-long-time-Appendix of arXiv:2605.16963, 'Stochastic Euler Equations with Pseudo-differential Noise: Continuous and Discontinuous Pe'] Let the conditions of Theorem (Thm-local-Appendix of the paper) hold. Let  
		$\frac{d}{2}+p<\theta<s-\max \{3(\alpha\lor \beta\lor \varsigma),\ell\mathbf{1}_{\{\epsilon>0\}},1\}$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf{(\arabic*)}},leftmargin=0.79cm]\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			\item  Under (Hypo-DNI-1 F-h of the paper), the system (equation SPDE-general of the paper) with initial data $u(0)=u_0$ admits a global $H^s$ solution satisfying
			\begin{equation*}
				\mathbb{E} \left[V(\|u(t)\|_{H^s}^2)\Big|\mathcal{F}_0\right]  
				\leq \Big(V(\|u_0\|^2_{H^s})+\mathscr{G}_2t\Big) {\rm e}^{\mathscr{G}_1t},
				\quad t>0.
			\end{equation*}
			Moreover, the solution map $H^{s,\theta}\ni u_0\mapsto u(t)\in H^{s,\theta}$ is continuous, where $H^{s,\theta}$ denotes the space $H^s$ equipped with the $H^{\theta}$-topology.
			
			\item   If (Hypo-DNI-1 F-h of the paper) is strengthened to (Hypo-DNI-2 F-h of the paper), then $u$ satisfies 
			\begin{equation*} 
				\mathbb{E}\left[V(\|u(t)\|_{H^s}^2) \Big| \mathcal{F}_0\right]  
				\leq V(\|u_0\|^2_{H^s}), \qquad t\ge0.
			\end{equation*}
			Moreover, the problem (equation SPDE-general of the paper) on $\mathbb T^d$ admits an invariant measure $\mu$ in the sense of Definition (IM definition of the paper) with $E=H^s$. 
			
			\item  If (Hypo-DNI-3 F-h of the paper) holds, then  
			\begin{equation*} 
				\int_0^t\mathbb{E}  \left[V\left(\frac{\|u(t')\|^2_{W^{p,\infty}}}{M^2}\right)\Bigg|\mathcal{F}_0\right]{\,\rm{d}} t'
				\leq  \frac{V(\| u_0\|^2_{H^\theta})}{\mathscr{G}_3}\left(1-{\rm e}^{-\mathscr{G}_3t}\right),
				\quad t>0.
			\end{equation*}
			As a result, the Dirac measure centered at $0$ is the \textbf{unique invariant probability measure} on both $\mathbb T^d$ and $\mathbb R^d$ when $h(0)=0$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and let X^L denote X with the coordinates in a block L replaced by an independent copy. Then (X, X^L) is an exchangeable pair, and E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L). Consequently E[(X - X^L)^2] <= 4 Var(X) always, and E[(X - X^L)^2] <= 2 Var(X) whenever Cov(X, X^L) >= 0. The identity requires no independence beyond that of the resampled block and no structure on X beyond square-integrability.

In the width-one strip of the exact-variance lemma, perturb all Gaussian vertex weights by g^s=e^(-s)g+sqrt(1-e^(-2s))g' with independent copy g'. The number B_r(s) of diamonds where the maximizing choice differs has Binomial(r,q(s)) law, q(s)=arccos(e^(-s))/pi. The probability of identical maximizing paths is (1-q(s))^r, and their expected shared-vertex fraction is 1-rq(s)/(2r+1). For s=r^(-alpha) with fixed 0<alpha<2, the path-equality probability tends to zero, shared fraction tends to one, and Var(M_r) remains linear in r. This refutes only the unqualified path-change auxiliary bridge.
All assumptions of the width-one exact-variance lemma
Independent Gaussian copy in the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck perturbation
Fixed alpha in (0,2) for the asymptotic claim

If ||E_0||_2=q<1, then ||X_t-B^(-1)||_2 <= ||B^(-1)||_2 q^(2^t), hence X_t converges to B^(-1). The source initialization X_0=alpha B^T satisfies q<1 whenever 0<alpha<2/lambda_max(B^T B). The residual identity itself holds for arbitrary square B and X_t; invertibility and the strict contraction condition are required for this inverse-convergence conclusion.

Let n,d>=1 and T>=2 be integers, and m>=1 an integer factor width. Fix tokens x_it in R^d, queries z_i in R^d, labels Y_i in {-1,+1}, and a linear head v in R^d. Select opt_i in argmax_t Y_i v^T x_it. Let C be the set of real d-by-d matrices satisfying (x_i,opt_i-x_it)^T W z_i>=1 for all i and t!=opt_i. Consider (Att-SVM), minimizing ||W||_F over C, and (Att-SVM-star), minimizing ||W||_* over C subject to rank(W)<=m. The nuclear norm ||W||_* is the sum of singular values. For each problem separately assume its feasible set is nonempty. Every global optimizer W of either problem has row(W) contained in S=span{z_1,...,z_n}. Consequently rank(W)<=dim(S)<=min(n,d), with the additional rank cap m in the nuclear problem. No uniqueness is asserted for nuclear-norm optimizers. The conclusion concerns global solutions of these margin problems, not arbitrary KKT points or gradient-descent limits.
finite real dataset and fixed linear head; opt_i chosen by token scores
nonempty feasible set for the particular stated optimization problem
global optimum, not merely a stationary point; nuclear problem retains rank cap m

body:
[Theorem 1 (EPI on compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a compact and metrizable topological abelian group, equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Assume that $G$ has no open subgroups except $G$ itself and possibly $\{0\}$. Let $X,Y$ be independent random variables on $G$ with finite entropies. Then
$$h(X+Y)-\frac{1}{2}h(X)-\frac{1}{2}h(Y) \geq 0.$$
Moreover:
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(i)$]
If $G$ is connected, then there is equality if and only 
if $X$ and $Y$ are both uniform on $G$.
\item[$(ii)$]
If $G$ is finite, then there is equality if and only if 
either both $X$ and $Y$ are uniform on the whole group $G$ 
or both $X$ and $Y$ are deterministic.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: EPI on compact groups

[Definition 6 (Rhombus concavity) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{def:rhomb}
Given a function $h:T \ra \R$, and a positive integer $n$,  let $h_n$ denote the function from $T_n$ to $\R$ such that for $(nx, ny) \in T_n$, $h_n(nx, ny) = n^2 h(x, y).$
A function $h:T \ra \R$ is called {\bf rhombus concave} if for any positive integer $n$, 
and any $i$, $\De_i h_n$ is nonpositive on $E_i(T_n),$ and $h$ is continuous on $T$.
The corresponding function $h_n$ is called {\bf discrete (rhombus) concave}.  
Note that a necessary and sufficient condition for a function $h_n$ from $T_n$ to $\R$ to be discrete concave,  is that the piecewise linear extension (which we denote $\tilh_n$) of $h_n$ to $nT$ is  concave.
Here each piece is an isosceles right triangle with a $\sqrt{2}-$length  hypotenuse parallel to the vector $(1, 1).$
title: Rhombus concavity

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Set
\(
  U_1
  :=
  |\Phi_1|_{\sigma_0}^2
  =
  \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}.
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
  \dot H_0=0,
  \qquad
  \ddot H_0
  =
  -4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $k\ge 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \sigma_0
  +2t\operatorname{Re}\Phi_1
  \\
  &+
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \left[
    2\operatorname{Re}\Phi_2
    +
    \left(
      2U_1-4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1
    \right)\sigma_0
  \right]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}
Here $O_{C^k}(t^3)$ means that, after subtracting the displayed
terms up to order two, the remainder $R_t$ satisfies
\(
  \|R_t\|_{C^k(X_0,\sigma_0)}\le C_k |t|^3
\)
for $|t|$ sufficiently small. Equivalently, all covariant derivatives
of $R_t$ up to order $k$, computed with respect to $\sigma_0$, are
uniformly $O(t^3)$.
Equivalently, in the coordinate $z$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  +
  t\left(
    \phi_1\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_1}\,d\bar z^2
  \right)
  +
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \Bigg[
    \phi_2\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_2}\,d\bar z^2
  \\
  &+
    \left\{
      \frac{2|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      -
      4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}
      \left(
        \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      \right)
    \right\}
    \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  \Bigg]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}

body:
Let Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n (the centred cube of volume 1), n >= 2. For every unit vector a in R^n, 1 <= vol_{n-1}(Q_n \cap a^perp) <= sqrt(2). The upper bound is attained exactly when a = (+-e_i +- e_j)/sqrt(2) (for example the hyperplane orthogonal to (1,1,0,...,0)); the lower bound 1 (Hadwiger, Hensley; Ball gives a simpler proof) exactly when a = +-e_j. Probabilistic form: if U_1,...,U_n are independent and uniform on [-1/2,1/2] and a_1^2 + ... + a_n^2 = 1, the density of a_1U_1 + ... + a_nU_n is largest at 0, where it equals vol_{n-1}(Q_n \cap a^perp); so this density is at most sqrt(2), with equality for (U_1 + U_2)/sqrt(2).

Assumes: central sections (hyperplanes through the centre of the cube); cube normalised to volume 1: Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n; the density statement is for independent uniform inputs

\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $d(\triangle)$ is odd and $\mathsf{E}_S(\triangle)$ holds, does $\mathsf{E}_S(\boxtimes)$ hold?

    \item If $S$ is consistent, $d(\triangle)$ is odd, and $p$ is a fixed point of $\triangle v$, then is $p$ non-refutable in $S$?
\end{enumerate} (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

UNREVIEWED DRAFT; independent referee pending. The conditional two-Cardy-martingale identification route does not prove square-bond conformal invariance by itself. Its model-specific input is a construction of correctly oriented square-bond Doob crossing or exit martingales P_delta,i and, on each nondegenerate stopped exploration interval, an approximation E[sup |P_delta,i-C(X_delta/Y_delta,i)|] tending to zero, together with joint driver/marked-point convergence, compatible limiting filtration and stopping/boundary control. Here C(u) is the normalized integral of [v(1-v)]^(-2/3) from 0 to u. This input is UNPROVED in the reviewed route. Fixed-domain pointwise limits alone cannot justify evaluation at varying random slit domains.
Actual discrete event and primal/dual boundary convention must be specified
Both martingales use one exploration filtration
Curve-to-driver compatibility and joint convergence are additional obligations

body: Coarea bound for a definite rank-two core. If (Y_1, Y_2) has density rho on R^2 and lambda_1, lambda_2 > 0, then S = lambda_1 Y_1^2 + lambda_2 Y_2^2 has density p_S(s) = (2 sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2))^{-1} int_0^{2 pi} rho(sqrt(s/lambda_1) cos th, sqrt(s/lambda_2) sin th) d th <= pi ||rho||_inf/sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2) (substitute u = sqrt(lambda_1) y_1, v = sqrt(lambda_2) y_2 and use polar coordinates; in two dimensions the length of the level curve and the gradient cancel, which is why ||rho||_inf suffices, and in three dimensions this fails). For an orthonormal two-dimensional projection of independent coordinates with densities <= 1, ||rho||_inf <= 2 (Livshyts-Paouris-Pivovarov), attained by ((X_1 + X_2)/sqrt2, (X_3 + X_4)/sqrt2) with uniform laws on unit intervals, so a definite rank-two core has density <= 2 pi/sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2). Passing from the core to the full form Q = core + R, with R depending on the same coordinates, is where the conjecture is hard.

body: In mathematical logic, the compactness theorem states that a set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of it has a model. This theorem is an important tool in model theory, as it provides a useful method for constructing models of any set of sentences that is finitely consistent.

[Theorem thm:MKT-moment of arXiv:2412.01015, 'Classical beta ensembles and related eigenvalues processes at high temperature and the Mar'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}$ with all finite moments
\[
	p_m = \int u^m d\mu(u) < \infty, \quad m = 0, 1,2,\dots.
\]
For $c > 0$,
define the sequence $\{h_n\}_{n \ge 0}$ by the moment relation~(equation moment-MKR of the paper).
Then $\nu = {\mathcal M}_{c}(\mu)$ has moments $\{h_n\}$. Consequently, when two probability measures $\nu$ and $\mu$ are determined by moments, the above moment relation holds, if and only if $\nu = {\mathcal M}_{c}(\mu)$.
title: Theorem thm:MKT-moment of arXiv:2412.01015

[Theorem thm:exchangeable-reserve of arXiv:2608.20480, 'When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone \\ Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification'] Let $d_{\mathrm{DS}}(\mathcal{H})=d<\infty$. Suppose that among the examples received by the learner are $r$ clean examples $Z_1,\ldots,Z_r$, and let $Z_0$ be a fresh clean example. Assume that, after fixing all remaining examples and the clean information used to choose them, the examples $Z_0,Z_1,\ldots,Z_r$ remain exchangeable. Then the canonical one-inclusion learner satisfies
\[
    \mathbb{E} L_D(\widehat h,h^\star)
    \le
    \frac{d}{r+1}.
\]
The learner need not be told which observed examples constitute the exchangeable reserve. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Fix 0<kappa<1/4. On Z^2 consider the homogeneous kernel

p(+e_1)=1/4+delta, p(-e_1)=1/4-delta,
p(+e_2)=p(-e_2)=1/4,

where 0<delta<=1/4-kappa. Its environment law is a Dirac mass at that row at each site, hence is spatially iid and kappa-uniformly elliptic. Its increments are iid. The strong law gives X_n/n -> (2delta,0), so it is directionally transient and ballistic in e_1. Nevertheless

sup_{0<delta<=1/4-kappa} E_0[sum_{n>=0} 1_{X_n=0}] = infinity,

The elementary central-binomial lower bound binom(2n,n)>=4^n/(2sqrt(n)) follows by induction from n=1, since

binom(2n+2,n+1)/binom(2n,n)=4(1-1/(2n+2))
and (1-1/(2n+2))^2 >= n/(n+1).

Every path of length 2n under p_delta has probability at least (1-4delta)^(2n) times its p_0 probability. If delta<=1/(16N) and n<=N, Bernoulli's inequality gives (1-4delta)^(2n)>=1-8delta n>=1/2. Therefore its Green function is at least

1 + (1/8) sum_{n=1}^N 1/n.

Choose delta_N=min((1/4-kappa)/2,1/(16N)); these are positive, preserve the same ellipticity lower bound, and give the divergent harmonic lower bound.

P_delta(X_n=0) <= E_delta exp(-theta X_n^(1))
 = [1/2+2sqrt(1/16-delta^2)]^n.

Let (X,d) be a compact metric space of diameter at most one, with covering numbers N(X,epsilon)<=epsilon^(-d_x) for 0<epsilon<=1, where d_x>0. Let P be a Borel probability measure, and W:X x X->[0,cmax] a measurable symmetric kernel with 0<cmin<=d_P(x)=integral W(x,y)dP(y) and cmax<=1. Assume there is ONE partition X=X_1 union ... union X_q into q>=1 measurable pieces such that |W(x,y)-W(xprime,y)|<=cLip d(x,xprime) for every y and every x,xprime in the same piece. Let x_1,...,x_n be independent samples from P, and fix 0<rho<=1/2. For any fixed bounded Borel f:X->R, define T_X f(x)=n^(-1)sum_i W(x,x_i)f(x_i) and T_P f(x)=integral W(x,y)f(y)dP(y). There is a universal C such that, with probability at least 1-rho, sup_x |T_X f(x)-T_P f(x)| <= C ||f||_sup [cLip sqrt(d_x)+(cmax+cLip)sqrt(log(q/rho))]/sqrt(n). The card uses a common partition explicitly; it does not assert this bound merely from separate, y-dependent partitions. The confidence range rho<=1/2 is retained to absorb the standard two-sided tail constants.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation or source-specific limiting obstruction Result: Linear Debye screening gives the formal structure factor S(k)=|k|^2/(|k|^2+m^2), with m^2 proportional to beta times the background density. Its truncated-correlation Fourier transform is proportional to -m^2/(|k|^2+m^2). In two dimensions the inverse transform is a multiple of the modified Bessel function K0(m*r), whose large-distance behavior is proportional to exp(-m*r)/sqrt(m*r). Check: The resolvent of -Delta+m^2 has Fourier multiplier1/(|k|^2+m^2); its heat-kernel integral yields the positive radial K0 kernel. Thus screening formally creates an exponential length m^-1 rather than a Riesz power tail. Obstruction: The linear-response closure is not proved for the interacting Gibbs law. A rigorous result needs a uniform control of nonlinear correlations and error terms at distances beyond the screening length. The calculation identifies a mechanism, not a clustering theorem.

A continuous planar path and its one-dimensional polygonal approximations do not by themselves produce a one-dimensional Jordan arc contained in the path image. For the standard Koch arc, the similarity dimension is log(4)/log(3)>1 and every nontrivial internal Jordan arc has that dimension. This deterministic obstruction refutes the generic polygonal-approximation route; it asserts no dimension above one for a Brownian trace.
The standard Koch arc satisfies the stated self-similar Jordan-arc hypotheses
The usual open-set self-similar dimension theorem is an input

body: In combinatorial mathematics and extremal set theory, the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that every family of sets with small VC dimension consists of a small number of sets. Here, the VC dimension is the largest size $k$ of a set with the property that all of its subsets can be formed by intersecting it with a member of the family. If the family has $n$ elements in its union, then the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that its number of sets is at most proportional to $n^{k}$.

[Proposition 12 (Risk recursion for Polyak) of arXiv:2609.02728, 'Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improv'] Under the gradient-noise covariance assumption, the expected excess risk obeys the two-sided recursion:
\begin{equation} 
    \EE[\cE(\btheta_k)]
    \eqsim
    \cS_{\polyak}(k)
    +
    \frac{\eta^2\sigma^2}{B}\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\mathcal{K}_{\polyak}(\tau)
    +
    \frac{\eta^2}{B}\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\mathcal{K}_{\polyak}(\tau)\EE[\cE(\btheta_{k-1-\tau})].
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the right-hand side provides both rigorous upper and lower bounds for the expected excess risk up to universal constant factors.

body:
[Lemma lem:singleton-order-sum of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $\mathsf M_j$ be any typed passive copy of the coordinate pure-Weyl
multiplier in (lem:singleton-renewal of the paper), with arbitrary passive
Hilbert-space amplification.  Put
\[
 \mathsf V_j=\mathsf Q\mathsf M_j\mathsf Q,
 \qquad A_j=\mathscr E\mathsf M_j\mathscr T,
 \qquad \mathfrak H_a=\mathscr G\mathcal K^a\mathscr G^*.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathscr T^*\mathsf M_j\mathscr T
 =\mathscr E\mathsf M_j\mathscr E^*=0,
 \qquad
 \mathscr G^*\mathsf V_j\mathscr G
 =-\mathcal KA_j-A_j^*\mathcal K.
\tag{3.2.10q$_1$}
\]
There is a numerical $C$ such that
\[
 \sum_{a,b\ge0}
 \|\mathfrak H_a\mathsf V_j\mathfrak H_b\|
 \le C\frac{\log(n+2)}{\sqrt n}.
\tag{3.2.10q$_2$}
\]
Consequently, for every fixed $L<\infty$ there is $A_L<\infty$ such
that a passive-singleton component with $2\le s\le L\log n$ labelled
vertices satisfies, after summing every strict chronological order and
every allowed finite-gap simplex,
\[
 \sum_{\sigma\in S_s}
 \|\mathcal X_{s,\sigma}\|
 \le \frac{A_L^s}{N}.
\tag{3.2.10q$_3$}
\]
After the proved circuit-anchored root/pass rewrite, its one free
translation, and a fixed terminal ribbon gluing, its scalar contribution is at most
$A_L^s(m/N)\mathfrak a_\Gamma$, where
$\mathfrak a_\Gamma$ is the positive projective majorant of the already
normalized non-temporal atom.
The same conclusion holds for several Haar-separated passive-singleton
components after their labelled vertex sets have been fixed, with one
factor $m/N$ per component and no interleaving multinomial.  This last
sentence does not sum over varying component-label decompositions; the
physical maximal passive-only components are instead annihilated exactly
in (lem:haar-passive-zero of the paper) below.

body: Publication record. In the critical beta-splitting random tree a clade of m leaves splits into clades of i and m - i leaves with probability proportional to 1/(i(m - i)); the drawn length of a binary tree is the total length of the vertical lines of its cladogram, each vertex drawn at the level of its height. Open Problem 14 of D. J. Aldous and S. Janson, The critical beta-splitting random tree II: overview and open problems, asks for a proof that the expected drawn length L_n grows roughly like n log^4 n. Y. Shmalo, The drawn length of the critical beta-splitting tree grows linearly (2026) shows instead that L_n/n converges to a finite constant lambda with 4.800 < lambda < 5.372 (lambda ≈ 4.88 numerically). Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/beta-splitting-drawn-length (commit 536da55fafcf). Not refereed; an independent read is owed.
title: Aldous-Janson Open Problem 14 (critical beta-splitting tree) answered: the expected drawn length grows linearly, L_n/n -> lambda with 4.800 < lambda < 5.372, not like n log^4 n (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/beta-splitting-drawn-length)

Own-work auxiliary proof draft (unaudited); no novelty priority claimed. Fix any oracle O. Let P_L be given by a uniform polynomial-time O-relative evaluator of nonnegative rational weights with polynomial numerator/denominator bit bounds and positive normalizer. Suppose a polynomial-size nonuniform dyadic AR proposal R_L has polynomial next-bit precision and P_L(x)<=D(L)R_L(x) pointwise, for an integer-valued polynomial D>=1. For every fixed positive integer c there is a polynomial-size nonuniform dyadic AR Q_L with KL(P_L||Q_L)<L^(-c). Conditional importance sampling with K=(1024 D L^(2c+2))^2 samples per position, globally shared random tapes, and one dyadic normalizer-scale exponent suffices; smoothing and output rounding bound KL by (47/120)L^(-c). Exact normalization, a sampler for P and distributional inversion are not assumed. The domination premise itself also yields nonuniform inverse-polynomial-TV sampling by bounded rejection. No common oracle with NP circuit hardness and domination proposals for all efficiently weighted laws has been constructed. This does not settle Target 2 or assert that the premise follows from IR2.
Uniform polynomial-time O-relative rational weight evaluator; known polynomial numerator/denominator bit bound; Z_L>0

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:7f48ea00b06eac61a7d3de865d18e29f986464964f5d95df60f3913c79888486","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/7f/7f48ea00b06eac61a7d3de865d18e29f986464964f5d95df60f3913c79888486.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e6f8938fd0964f6bdec71311b16a459f94b9a6dcb22372c6c194227f52f9e1ff","bundle_entry_key":"importance-weighted-dominated-autoregressive-proposals","bundle_id":"population.t410-importance-weighted-dominated-autoregressive-proposals","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"autoregressive distributions; importance sampling; oracle computational complexity; forward KL; nonuniform circuits","draft":"w739/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:complexity.cryptography:importance-weighted-dominated-autoregressive-proposals","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Polynomial domination by an AR proposal suffices for forward-KL approximation

T410-w739-C012 v1. Kind: auxiliary sufficient-condition lemma. Target: 2.
Status: proof (unaudited). Own-work draft; no novelty priority claimed.
This is an alternative sufficient condition, not a construction of the target oracle.

## Statement and unpaid obligation

Fix an oracle O. For each integer L>=1 let P_L(x)=w_L(x)/Z_L on
{0,1}^L. The nonnegative rational weights w_L are uniformly polynomial-time
computable relative to O, not all zero, and their numerator and positive
denominator have bit lengths at most a known polynomial b(L).

Assume a polynomial-size nonuniform oracle autoregressive proposal R_L:
its next-bit probabilities are exactly evaluable dyadics with common
precision B(L), a polynomial. Assume further that

    P_L(x) <= D(L) R_L(x) for every x,                         (1)

where D>=1 is an integer-valued polynomial. Then for each fixed positive
integer c there is a polynomial-size nonuniform oracle autoregressive Q_L
whose next-bit probabilities are dyadic and

    KL(P_L || Q_L) <= (47/120) L^(-c) < L^(-c).              (2)

Natural logarithms are used. All circuits use the same oracle O. Their
size exponent may depend on c and on the polynomial bounds. The uniform
weight evaluator is a single algorithm; the proposal and resulting Q may
have length-dependent advice. For any fixed positive real requested
exponent one can instead use its integer ceiling.

The hardest unpaid step for Target 2 is to construct ONE oracle with
NP^O not contained in P^O/poly and, for EVERY efficient-weight law, a
proposal satisfying (1). This proof supplies no such oracle or universal
proposal. It does not derive (1) from the reported IR2 result, assert
equivalence with C003's sampler/inverter criterion, or settle Target 2.

## 1. Only a short scale advice is needed

The weight representation implies 2^(-b)<=Z_L<=2^(b+L). Choose the
integer a=ceil(log_2 Z_L) as nonuniform advice and set A=2^a. Then

    Z_L <= A <= 2 Z_L,       z:=Z_L/A belongs to [1/2,1].

The signed exponent a uses O(log(b+L+1)) bits; the rational A itself has
polynomial representation length. We do NOT assume the exact rational Z
has polynomial bit length: arbitrary rational weight denominators need
not share a small common denominator.

For R(x)>0 put h(x)=w(x)/(A R(x)); set h=0 when R(x)=0. Domination
ensures P(x)=w(x)=0 on the latter set. Consequently

    0 <= h(x) <= D,          E_R h = z.

Computing h takes polynomial-size exact rational arithmetic: R(x) is a
product of L polynomial-bit dyadics, and w,A have polynomial bit length.
Hereafter L subscripts are omitted.

## 2. Conditional importance estimates and change of measure

For a prefix s of length i<L with R(s)>0, define

    a_s=E_R[h(X)|s],    b_s=E_R[h(X) 1{X_(i+1)=1}|s].

Then P(s)=R(s)a_s/z. When P(s)>0 the true next-bit probability is
p_s=b_s/a_s. Draw K independent suffix samples from R(.|s). This is an
exact ancestral sampler: each next-bit dyadic of precision B uses B fair
bits, so at most LB random bits per sample. Let ahat_s,bhat_s be the
sample means of h and h times the next-bit indicator. Define

    g_s=bhat_s/ahat_s if ahat_s>0; otherwise g_s=1/2.

We always have 0<=g_s<=1 and ahat_s*g_s=bhat_s, including the zero
denominator case because nonnegative h forces bhat_s=0 there. Thus

    a_s |g_s-p_s| <= |a_s-ahat_s|+|b_s-bhat_s|.             (3)

This follows by writing a_s*g_s-b_s as
(a_s-ahat_s)*g_s+(bhat_s-b_s). Each sample variable lies in [0,D], so
variance of each mean is at most D^2/K. By Cauchy-Schwarz its mean
absolute error is at most D/sqrt(K). Multiply (3) by R(s)/z and sum over
prefixes with P(s)>0. Since their R masses sum to at most one and z>=1/2,

    sum_s P(s) E |g_s-p_s| <= 4D/sqrt(K)                   (4)

at every position. Prefixes of zero P mass contribute zero. At an
R-null prefix output 1/2 directly; it is P-null by (1).

No sample from P, normalizer computation, or distributional inversion
was used. In particular we did not require an accuracy guarantee at
each one of exponentially many prefixes.

## 3. One polynomial table of shared tapes

At each position select K independent tapes of length LB. Use these
SAME tapes to evaluate the conditional sampler at every prefix of that
length. For each FIXED prefix its K samples have exactly the independent
law used above. Evaluations at different prefixes may be correlated;
only linearity of expectation over prefixes is used in (4).

There are L*K*L*B advice bits, not a tape table indexed by all prefixes.
For any fixed advice table, evaluation runs K ancestral samplers and
computes their exact rational sample means. Adding K polynomial-bit
rationals can increase bit length by at most a polynomial factor K;
division and the other arithmetic therefore have polynomial circuits.
This remains true when the proposal itself has nonuniform advice.

## 4. Smoothing, KL, and explicit sample count

Write eta=L^(-c), epsilon=eta/(16L), and choose the perfect square

    K = (1024 D L^(2c+2))^2.

This is polynomial for fixed c. Let q_s=epsilon+(1-2epsilon)g_s at
R-positive prefixes, so q_s is in [epsilon,1-epsilon]. Also

    |p_s-q_s| <= |p_s-g_s|+epsilon,
    (p_s-q_s)^2 <= 2|p_s-g_s|+2epsilon^2.

For Bernoulli parameters p in [0,1], q in (0,1), the inequality
log t<=t-1, applied to each nonzero P term, gives

    kl(p||q) <= (p-q)^2/[q(1-q)].                          (5)

The same formula holds at p=0,1 by the zero-mass convention. Chain rule
for forward KL, (4), and (5) yield

    E KL(P||Q) <= [8DL/sqrt(K)+2L epsilon^2]
                         /[epsilon(1-epsilon)].          (6)

Here sqrt(K)=64DL/(eta epsilon). Each of the two terms in (6) equals
eta/[8(1-epsilon)]. Since epsilon<=1/16, their sum is at most
(4/15)eta. This calculation averages over a finite, polynomial-length
random table, not over independent conditional errors along a P path.

## 5. Polynomial-bit dyadic outputs

Choose an integer t with Delta=2^(-t)<=eta epsilon/(16L), for example
t=ceil(log_2(256 L^(2c+2))). Replace q_s by

    qhat_s = floor(2^t q_s)/2^t.

Then |qhat_s-q_s|<=Delta and qhat_s>=epsilon/2, while both complementary
probabilities are at least epsilon/2. The derivative of log on this
range is at most 2/epsilon. For every fixed random table, each next-bit
log probability changes in absolute value by at most 2Delta/epsilon.
The chain rule therefore gives

    KL(P||Qhat) <= KL(P||Q)+2L Delta/epsilon
                <= KL(P||Q)+eta/8.

Use qhat=1/2 at R-null prefixes. Averaging shows

    E KL(P||Qhat) <= (4/15+1/8)eta = (47/120)eta.

Some single finite table has loss at most this average. Fix it as advice.
The resulting Qhat is a normalized AR law with polynomial-size oracle
circuits and t-bit dyadic next probabilities. This proves (2).

## Scope and validation

The proposal premise already implies NONUNIFORM approximate sampling of
P, although the proof above does not invoke such a sampler. Indeed draw
X from R and accept it with probability h(X)/D, using a fresh uniform
number in [0,1]. The acceptance probability is z/D>=1/(2D), and the
accepted law is exactly P. Rational acceptance probabilities can instead
be rounded DOWN to dyadics of mesh delta. The acceptance probability
decreases by at most delta and the accepted law changes in total
variation by at most 2D delta, provided delta<=1/(4D): if v(x) is the
unnormalized accepted mass and v'(x)<=v(x), their missing total mass e
is at most delta, and TV(v/alpha,v'/(alpha-e))<=e/alpha<=2D delta.
The rounded success probability is at least 1/(4D). Truncating after
T independent proposals adds at most (1-1/(4D))^T to the TV error.
For a requested inverse-polynomial error rho, choose dyadic
delta<=rho/(4D) and T>=4D ln(2/rho). Thus a strict polynomial-time
NONUNIFORM dyadic sampler with TV error at most rho follows. Its
normalizer-scale advice and the proposal advice need not be uniform.
This implication is an explicit limitation of the sufficient condition,
not a contradiction to it or a uniform sampling theorem for the oracle.

This proof is a sufficient-condition derivation, not a novelty claim or
an independently checked proof. Finite rational diagnostics check (3),
the prefix change-of-measure identity, and the constants, with an omitted-
denominator negative control. They do not prove the asymptotic theorem
by enumeration. No enormous K sample run is proposed or performed.
The condition (1) must be established before applying this to any
particular oracle or weight family. Target 1 C001 v2 remains subject to
independent review; Target 2 remains OPEN.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:cd6159c155b54a445d85ded8bfe2169b8fbff887b41d8a66fa0cb61f5b912613","revision_digest":"sha256:f19892a156489aea3c44cdeab77ef7112d4b9e56b7b483fe2d21b6bdf47d45f1","source_id":"own-work:T410-w739-C012-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T22:53:13.841333+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 201 (Identification of the most difficult error terms in the commuted wave equations) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\velocityarray \eqdef (v^1,v^2,v^3)$ 
be solutions to the covariant wave equations \eqref{E:COVARIANTWAVEEQUATIONSWAVEVARIABLES}. We denote the product of $\upmu$ and the RHS of the covariant wave equation satisfied by 
$v^i$ by $\mathfrak{G}_{i}$, 
i.e., 
$\upmu \Box_{\gfour} v^i = \mathfrak{G}_{i}$. \begin{subequations}  
\begin{align} 
\upmu \Box_{\gfour} (\tanderY^{N-1} \Lunit v^i) 
& 
= 
\angrmd^{\sharp} v^i  \cdot \upmu \angrmd \tanderY^{N-1} \mytr_{\gtorus}\upchi 
+ 
\tanderY^{N-1} \Lunit \mathfrak{G}_{i} 
+ 
\HarmlessWave{N},	
	\\
\begin{split} 
\upmu \Box_{\gfour} (\tanderY^{N-1}\Yvf{A} v^i) 
& 
= 
(\muX v^i)  \tanderY^{N-1} \Yvf{A} \mytr_{\gtorus} \upchi 
+ 
(\Speed^{-2} X^A) \angrmd^{\sharp} v^i \cdot \upmu \angrmd \tanderY^{N-1} \mytr_{\gtorus}\upchi 
\\
& \ \
+ 
\tanderY^{N-1}\Yvf{A} \mathfrak{G}_{i} 
+ 
\HarmlessWave{N}. 
\end{split}
\end{align}Moreover, if $1 \leq N \leq \Ntop$ and $\tander^N$
denotes any order $N$ string of $\mathcal{P}_u$-tangent commutator
other than the ones appearing on LHSs~\eqref{E:TOPCOMMUTEDWAVELFIRSTTHENALLYS}--\eqref{E:TOPCOMMUTEDWAVEALLYS},
(i.e., if $\tander^N$ features at least two copies of $\Lunit$ or only a single $\Lunit$ but does not act first like it does in
\eqref{E:TOPCOMMUTEDWAVELFIRSTTHENALLYS}), 
then $\tander^N v^i$ obeys the following wave equation:
\begin{align} 
\upmu \Box_{\gfour} (\tander^N v^i) 
	& = 
	\tander^N \mathfrak{G}_i
	+ 
	\HarmlessWave{N}.
\end{align}
\end{subequations}

body:
Let Z be a random finite measure on D with total mass T>0 almost surely and 0<E[T]<infinity. Put U_A=Z(A)/T. Then E[Z(A)]/E[T]-E[U_A]=Cov(T,U_A)/E[T] for each measurable A. Consequently mean normalized measure equals normalized mean measure exactly when Cov(T,U_A)=0 for every A. Independence of total mass and normalized measure is sufficient but unnecessary: three equally likely outcomes T=(1,2,3), U_first=(1,0,1) on two sites give both averages (2/3,1/3), yet T and the normalized measure are dependent. No integrability or independence claim for DGFF extremal mass is inferred from this finite example.

[Thm 7 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional $(n \geq 2)$ forward complete Finsler metric measure manifold with $\Lambda_F<\infty$. Assume that $\mathbf{S}\geq -\vartheta$ for some $\vartheta \geq 0$.
Given constants $p \in (\frac{n}{2}, n]$, $\alpha\in [\frac{1}{2},1)$ and a fixed point $x_{0}\in M$. Then,  for $0 \leq r < R_{0}$ and an arbitrarily fixed point $x\in M$ satisfying that $d_{F}(x_{0}, x) \leq \Lambda_{F}^{-1}\left( R_{0}-r\right)$, there exist positive constants $D_{1}=D_{1}(n, p, \vartheta , R_{0})$ and $D_{2}=D_{2}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})$, such that, when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}<D_{1}^{-\frac{2p-1}{p}}$, we have
\beq
&& \left(\frac{m\left(B_{\Lambda_{F}^{-1}r}^{+}(x)\right)}{m\left(B_{R_{0}}^{+}(x_{0})\right)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2 p-1}} \geq  \Big[\frac{1}{4} \left(1-D_{1} \overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}\right)
e^{-\frac{\vartheta R_{0}}{2 p-1}}\Lambda_{F}^{-\left(2 \vartheta R_{0}b(p,\alpha)+\frac{5n}{2p-1}\right)}   \nonumber \\
&& \times \left(\frac{r}{R_{0}}\right)^{\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+\frac{4n-2p}{2p-1}}  -  \frac{D_{2}\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}}{1-D_{1} \overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}} \Big] \left(\frac{r}{R_{0}}\right)^{\frac{2p-n}{2p-1}}, 
\eeq
where
\beqn
&& D_{1}(n,p,\vartheta,R_{0}):=D(n, p) e^{\frac{2 p+1}{2 p-1} \vartheta R_{0}} R_{0}^{\frac{2p}{2 p-1}},  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ D(n, p):=\frac{n(n-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2 p-1}}(2 p-1)^{\frac{p}{2 p-1}}}{(2 p-n)^\frac{3p-2}{2p-1}},    \\
&& D_{2}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0}):=\frac{D_{1}(n,p,\vartheta,R_{0}) e^{\frac{\vartheta R_{0}}{2 p-1}} \Lambda_{F}^{-\frac{2p-n}{2p-1}}}{1-e^{-\frac{\vartheta R_{0}}{2p-1}}(2-\alpha)^{\frac{2p-2n}{2p-1}}\alpha^{\frac{n}{2p-1}} }, \ \ \  b(p,\alpha):=\frac{1}{(2p-1)\ln(2-\alpha)}.
\eeqn

[Lemma 25 (Stage preparation, stability, and regular restart) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] There are constants
\[
        K_{\mathrm{st}}<\infty,\qquad \Lambda_*<\infty,
        \qquad \beta_{\mathrm{reg}}>0,\qquad C_{\mathrm{st}}<\infty,
\]
depending only on \(K,N,\sigma\), with the following property.  For every
\(0<\beta_*\leq\beta_{\mathrm{reg}}\), there is a constant
\(\eta_{\mathrm{st}}>0\), depending only on \(K,N,\sigma,\beta_*\), such that the following holds.
Let \(p(\tau)\) be any parabolically rescaled \(\delta_0\)-large block, for
some \(\delta_0\geq c_0\), under the standing fixed-threshold application.
Fix the torus structure used during this
stage and put
\[
        q(1)=p(1),\qquad r(1)=\overline{q(1)}.
\]
Put
\[
        b:=\|q(1)-r(1)\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,r(1))}.
\]
Assume that \(r(1)\) is Riemannian,
\(\BG_N(r(1);\Lambda_*)\) holds, and \(b<\eta_{\mathrm{st}}\).  These are
exactly the analytic start conditions in
Definition~\ref{def:admissible-stage-start}, with
\(\Lambda=\Lambda_*\) and \(\eta=\eta_{\mathrm{st}}\).
Then the invariant Ricci flow \(r(\tau)\) and the Ricci--DeTurck flow
\(q(\tau)\) relative to it exist on \([1,100]\), and
\begin{align}
        |\sec_{r(\tau)}|&\leq K_{\mathrm{st}}/\tau,
                &&1\leq\tau\leq100,                               \\
        \|q-r\|_{X_r^N[1,100]}
                &<\beta_*,                                         \\
        \|q-r\|_{X_r^N[1,100]}
                &\leq C_{\mathrm{st}}b.                                 
\end{align}
If
\[
        q^+(1)=100^{-1}q(100),\qquad
        \rho^+=100^{-1}r(100),\qquad
        r^+(1)=\overline{q^+(1)},
\]
then \(r^+(1)\) is Riemannian, \(\BG_N(r^+(1);\Lambda_*)\) holds,
\(|\sec_{r^+(1)}|\leq K_{\mathrm{st}}\), and
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
 &\|q^+(1)-\rho^+\|_{C^{N+5,\sigma}(M,\rho^+)}
 +\|r^+(1)-\rho^+\|_{C^{N+5,\sigma}(M,\rho^+)}\\
 &\qquad\leq C_{\mathrm{st}}b.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
        \|r^+(1)-\rho^+\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,\rho^+)}
        \leq C_{\mathrm{st}}b.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Abel's theorem (the Abelian direction): if the series sum a_n converges to s, then the power series f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1 and f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below. The converse is false in general: f(x) = sum (-1)^n x^n = 1/(1 + x) tends to 1/2 while sum (-1)^n diverges. Tauber's theorem (the Tauberian direction): if f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1, f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below, and n a_n -> 0, then sum a_n converges to s. Littlewood strengthened the condition to a_n = O(1/n) (Littlewood's Tauberian theorem, 1911), and Hardy and Littlewood showed that a one-sided bound n a_n >= -C also suffices. 'Abelian' theorems pass from a summability method's convergence to a weaker one; 'Tauberian' theorems go back under an extra growth condition on the terms.
Abel: sum a_n converges
Tauber: f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below and n a_n -> 0 (Littlewood: a_n = O(1/n) suffices, with a harder proof)

For |x| < 1, summation by parts gives sum_{n=0}^N a_n x^n = s_N x^N + (1 - x) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} s_n x^n, and letting N -> infinity (s_N is bounded and x^N -> 0) f(x) = (1 - x) sum_{n>=0} s_n x^n. Since (1 - x) sum x^n = 1, f(x) - s = (1 - x) sum (s_n - s) x^n. Given epsilon, choose N with |s_n - s| < epsilon for n > N; the tail is bounded by epsilon (1 - x) sum x^n = epsilon, and the finite head (1 - x) sum_{n <= N} (s_n - s) x^n tends to 0 as x -> 1. Write rho_i = ||f(x_i) - y_i|| / m_i for the per-row ratio. Then S = mean rho_i and Q = mean rho_i^2 = (mean rho_i)^2 + var(rho_i). Two estimators f and g with the same S can differ in Q by the difference of their ratio variances, and an estimator with the smaller Q can have the larger S whenever its ratios are less dispersed but larger on average - the ordering by Q is the ordering by S only when the ratio dispersion is comparable across candidates. Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph, q>=2 an integer, K>=0, u the uniform independent q-color law, and gamma_K the free ferromagnetic Potts law proportional to exp(K times the number of agreeing edges). Then D(u||gamma_K)>=|E|[log((exp(K)+q-1)/q)-K/q]. Equality holds on forests; for K>0 and a graph with a cycle it is strict. Thus on growing Z^d boxes at any fixed K>0, liminf D(u||gamma_K)/|V|>=d[log((exp(K)+q-1)/q)-K/q]>0. This is a product-law obstruction and does not establish critical discontinuity.
